title: Mating system of free-ranging domestic dogs and its consequences for dog evolution
abstract: The polygamous mating system of free-ranging domestic dogs (FRDs) contrasts with the social monogamy typical of gray wolves and all other wild canids. The transition to polygamy in dogs could have been initiated by a shift from apex predator to human commensal during the early domestication stages. Here, we test this hypothesis by investigating the characteristics of the FRD mating system that could have been important for domestication. This inference is based on genome-wide Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) data from three geographically distinct populations, including behavioral data for one of them. The reconstructed genealogies form a wide network of kinship relationships resulting from the frequent occurrence of maternal and paternal half-siblings, reflecting male and female polygamy. Reproductive success is positively correlated with the strength of social interactions and the number of connections with opposite-sex individuals, implying a preference toward familiar mates and the importance of social relationships in determining mating patterns. This is supported by a nonrandom distribution of reproductive partners and a reproductive skew in males and females. Multiple paternity within litters points to female polygamy within a single estrus, and sexual size dimorphism implies sexual selection favoring larger males. Physiological changes resulting from polygamy, including increased male fertility and reduced breeding seasonality, could have facilitated the natural spread of novel adaptive traits and limited the introgression from wolves. The change in reproductive patterns, typically considered a consequence of selective breeding, could instead have occurred naturally in response to the dietary niche change, triggering further changes that facilitated the domestication process.

title: “You Don’t Want to Drink? What Are You, Pregnant?!”
abstract: Background and objective Pregnant women, women of childbearing age, and their partners frequently report obtaining information about alcohol use during pregnancy from the mass media. Relying on mainstream media sources, such as television, can be problematic when the information presented is inaccurate, contributing to inconsistent messaging about the ‘safety’ of alcohol use during pregnancy. In the current study, we aimed to explore the portrayal of alcohol (and substance) use (e.g., tobacco, opioids) during pregnancy in North American, English speaking mainstream prime time and streaming television shows ( N = 25). To the authors’ knowledge, no previous study has explored the representations of alcohol (and/or substance use) during pregnancy in this context. Materials and methods The following inclusion criteria guided the show selection: (1) top 100 shows on cable/streaming services targeting women aged 18 to 49 years, and (2) shows suggested by targeted social media posts. Using ethnographic content analysis (ECA), the content and role of television media narratives in the social construction of alcohol meanings concerning the safety of alcohol use during pregnancy were explored. Results and conclusion In line with ECA, the results and conclusion are discussed together. The results and discussion are presented under an overarching narrative, the dichotomy of women's alcohol and substance use, which illustrates the sociocultural construction of alcohol and substance use during pregnancy. Within this overarching narrative, we focus on two sub-narratives: (1) women's acceptable use and (2) women's villainous use. Our analysis indicates misrepresentations regarding the safety of alcohol use during conception (e.g., Friends from College) and pregnancy (e.g., How I Met Your Mother, The Mindy Project). In addition, a narrative was identified relating to the difficulty of keeping a pregnancy private when not drinking socially (e.g., Friends, The Office). These narratives reinforced a dichotomy between the types of women who drink during pregnancy, including some for whom it was okay to have ‘just a little bit’ (e.g., How I Met Your Mother, The Big Bang Theory, Black Mirror) in contrast to others who were portrayed as villains who engaged in binge drinking behaviour and/or other comorbid substance use (e.g., Grey's Anatomy, Private Practice, Chicago Med, Law & Order). These results demonstrate the need to provide a clear, consistent messaging about the risks of alcohol use during pregnancy, as mixed messages from television can contribute to misinformation. The recommendations for messaging, as well as changing our approaches to fetal alcohol spectrum disorder prevention in the light of these findings are discussed.

title: Iran rebuilds family planning services.
abstract: After the revolution, the Islamic Republic of Iran instituted pronatalist policies which included lowering the minimum marriage age for girls to 9 years, abolishing some laws securing women's rights, and limiting availability of family planning (FP) services. By 1983, Iran's population growth rate was 3.9% which was among the highest worldwide. Before the revolution, Iran had 37 million people. About 2 million more people were added each year, resulting in a population size of 60 million by 1992. By the mid-1980s, economic development stood idle, there were not enough houses, children attended schools on 3 shifts, and malnutrition was spreading. In 1989, the government formed a population council and reestablished FP services. It also increased the minimum age of marriage for girls to 13 years, slightly improved women status, and eliminated fertility incentives for couples with at least 4 children. It also significantly increased funding for FP (from 560 million to 13 billion rials between 1990 and 1992). Government spending for FP will likely increase 2% annually until 2011. The government initiated a promotion of FP mass media campaign, emphasizing a 2-child family. Some posters showed a family with 2 girls. The mass media campaign promoted specific contraceptive methods (even tubal occlusion and vasectomy), a practice other Middle Eastern countries not do. 80% of sterilization acceptors claimed to learn about sterilization from the radio or newspapers. The Ministry of Health has invited the Association for Voluntary Surgical Contraception (AVSC) to help with its campaign to update sterilization techniques, including the non scalpel vasectomy technique. AVSC hopes to become even more involved in helping Iran update its national FP program.

title: Planning of Births and Childhood Undernutrition in Nepal: Evidence from a 2016 National Survey
abstract: Abstract Background Childhood undernutrition is a significant public health issue in low-and middle-income countries, including Nepal. However, there is limited evidence showing the association between the planning of birth (PoB) and childhood undernutrition (stunting and underweight). We aim to investigate the relationship between PoB and childhood undernutrition in the current study. Methods We used the Nepal Demographic Health Survey 2016 data, which is a nationally representative cross-sectional household survey. We used two common anthropometric indicators of childhood undernutrition as the outcome of this study. PoB is the main predictor of interest. Binary logistic regression with sampling weights was used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals to examine the association between the PoB and childhood undernutrition. Results The overall prevalence of stunting was 35.8%, and underweight was 27.1% in under-five children in Nepal. We found a higher rate of stunting (52.7%) and underweight (41.1%) in children with birth order > 3 and < 2 years of interval between birth and subsequent birth (IBBSB). The association between the birth order of children and the prevalence of undernutrition had strong statistical significance (p < 0.001). Mother’s age at marriage (p = 0.001), underweight mother (p < 0.001), mother’s education (p < 0.001), father’s education (p < 0.001), wealth quintile (p < 0.001), no exposure to mass media (p < 0.001), children’s age (p < 0.001), area of residence(p = 0.001) were significantly associated with childhood undernutrition. The result of the multiple logistic regression showed that children with birth order one and 12–24 months of interval between marriage and first birth (IBMFB) had significantly decreased odds of stunting as compared to those children with birth order one and < 12 months of IBMFB (OR 0.6, 95% CI 0.4–0.9). Conclusion The findings of the study demonstrate that PoB has a protective effect on childhood undernutrition. Delaying of childbirth until 12–24 months after marriage was found to be associated with reduced odds of childhood stunting. To mitigate childhood undernutrition, Nepal’s government needs to promote delayed childbearing after marriage while focusing on uplifting the household economics status and wide coverage of and utilization of mass media.

title: The Impact of Gender Factor on the Formation of Career Aspirations of Military Personnel of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
abstract: The article aims to identify the socio-psychological factors that determine the role of gender in the career aspirations of Ukrainian military personnel who are representatives of Generation Z. The study uses the psycholinguistic research method, specifically a free association experiment. Two stimulus words were selected for the psycholinguistic experiment: ‘career’ and ‘family’. The word ‘family’ serves as an auxiliary stimulus in the experiment. The study findings show that primary career motivation for both male and female respondents is the acquisition of social prestige, demonstrated through high status and rank identification, as well as a stable financial situation. Gender differences in career orientation lead to variations in conflict behavior strategies. Both men and women may use cooperation and competition strategies equally. However, in situations of conflicting interests, women tend to orient their social interaction towards confrontation and antagonism. The majority of both male and female respondents view the family as a potential for career advancement. However, some male respondents may experience high inter-role conflict between work and family. Women have various methods of resolving the role conflict between work and family. These include remaining childless, delegating child-rearing duties to their parents, and minimizing work responsibilities to allocate their physical and psychological resources to their family. To create more opportunities for women’s career success, it is recommended that military organizations provide training in integrative career approaches that can help service women approach career development in terms of their professional competencies rather than gender role stereotypes.

title: Comparison of psychosocial impact of strabismus on pediatric and adult patients in India
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to compare the psychosocial impact of squint on children with that on adult patients in India. Materials and Methods: In this descriptive cross-sectional study, a twenty-question quality-of-life instrument ASO-20 was administered to patients with strabismus to study the psychosocial impact of strabismus on them. The results were compiled in an Excel sheet and analyzed statistically. Results: Thirty-two children (5–18 years) and 24 adults (>18 years) were included in the study. It was observed that all the adults responded that they always noticed that they have strabismus as against significantly less (81.25%) number of children who did so. Similarly, 75% of adults responded that strabismus affected their relations with other people, whereas only 37.5% of children felt that strabismus affected their relations with other people. While 95.83% of adults felt that opportunities (social interaction or at work) were fewer because of strabismus, only 37.5% of the children felt so. Similarly, while all the adults responded that they frequently imagined that other people were thinking about their eyes, only half of the children (56.25%) felt so. The difference is statistically significant. Significantly more (83.3%) adults responded that they had more difficulty in making friends because of strabismus, as against this, only one-fourth (25%) of the children felt so. The difference is statistically significant. Both the groups felt that strabismus bothered them, people noticed strabismus while interacting with them and they felt different (inferior) because of strabismus. Although the percentage who felt so was more in adults as compared to children, the difference was not statistically significant. Similarly, more children (75%) said that strabismus never hindered their performance as compared to adults (66.67%), however, the difference was not statistically significant. Conclusions: Strabismus has negative psychosocial effects on the affected individual which intensify with age.

title: Sexual activity among adolescent school girls in Kisumu County
abstract:
Background: Adolescents are beginning sexual activity at a young age; most of them have no knowledge on dangers of having unprotected sex. Understanding motives that drive young girls to begin having sex is crucial as it will help in implementing evidence based policies on adolescent reproductive health. 
Objective: To describe the circumstance and determinants of sexual debut and activity among school girls aged 13-15years in rural set up. 
Design: Cross-sectional descriptive study. 
Setting: Primary and Secondary schools in low socio economic (rural) area of Kisumu County. 
Participants: School going girls between 13-15years. 
Methods: Eligible girls who gave adolescent assent had their height and weight taken (for B.M.I), breast Tanner staging was done in a private area with a chaperon then the girls were allowed to answer a self administered questionnaire. 
Results: 
Sexual activity was generally low, only 22% of the participants had begun sexual activities. Seventy nine percent of sexual debuts took place in home set ups. Sexual debut with neighbors was the most common at 42% while only 4% of sexually experienced girls reported having sexual debut with a stranger. Whereas sex; suggestions (P value = 0.003), opinions about sexual status of their friends (P value <0.001) and drug use (P value = 0.02) were found to increase likelihood of engagement in sexual activities, religiosity (P value = 0.491) and single parented families (P value = 0.326) were. found not to have any risk reduction in this study. Contraceptive use among the sexual debutants was found to be low, only 22.1 % of the sexually active girls recalled using any form of contraception at sexual debut. Age of partners at sexual debut was on average two years older. Seventy nine percent of girls reported having been promised items during sexual debut, with money being the most promised item at 49%. 
Conclusion: 
Sexual activity among this age group was generally low. Contraceptive use at sexual debut was also low. Predictors of sexual activities included drut, use, suggestion from friends to have sex and opinion about their peers' sexual status. Peer influence was a big determinant of sexual activity. Sexual debut with strangers is rare. Partners of sexual debutant girls were on average 2 years older. 
Recommendations: 
Since the studied population was highly religious as shown by the number of times religious meetings were attended in the preceding month to this study, introduction of sex education in religious meetings from as early as preadolescent could provide an alternative way of educating this population. Drug use by teenagers has to be addressed as an urgent issue and priority Political good will in addressing issues like drug use and implementation of existing laws. An interesting finding in this study was the venue of sexual debut which has not been reported in many studies on adolescent sexuality hence, need for further studies specifically designed to investigate why homes were the preferred venues of sexual debut. Educating mothers on how to handle adolescent reproductive health issues should be encouraged as parents and more so mothers are the primary socializes of their adolescent daughters and need to have skills on how to handle the adolescent reproductive health 
matters. Promotion of awareness and utilization of youth friendly services to reduce idleness and engage in productive time spending activities.

title: DEMOGRAPHIC DETERMINANTS OF FORMATION AND USE OF HUMAN CAPITAL IN UKRAINE: DIFFERENTIAL ANALYSIS AND FORECAST
abstract: The article deals with the problem that is little investigated in domestic economics. It assesses the impact of demographic processes on the prospects of accumulation and productivity of human capital. The author argues that focusing only in the quality of education and training that is inherent in most modern research, minimizes the effectiveness of human capital management as an economic asset. A man is a demographic basis of human capital accumulation. Accordingly, the particular demographic processes such as fertility, mortality, migration, development and disintegration of families, require careful analysis. The main objectives of the study related to the specification of the impact of demographic situation on the effectiveness of formation and use of human capital. It was found that due to the increasing demographic crisis in Ukraine initial conditions of accumulation of human capital at all levels of the economic system deteriorated significantly. It was substantiated that the renovation of demographic policy is a key factor for improving the efficiency of social investment; it also causes optimization of relations in various spheres of social interaction.

title: Living with drought: climate change perceptions, adaptation, and mitigation among farmers in rural Bangladesh
abstract: The paper presents a new behavioural model that collectively focuses on how the smallholder farmers in the drought-prone Barind Tract of Bangladesh perceive, mitigate, and adapt with the effects of climate change. A survey of 385 farm households was examined with the help of linear and ordinal logistic regression models to point out socioeconomic institutional determinants of these behavioural reactions. Findings indicate that 46 per cent of farmers ( n = 177) had a moderate perception of climate change, which was related mostly to lowered soil fertility, water shortage and decreased crop production. Age, education, and income had a significant positive effect on climate awareness (R 2 = 0.692, p < 0.001), whereas agricultural extension, livestock ownership, and peer-to-peer learning had a positive effect on adaptive and mitigative abilities. Conversely, the lack of financial capacity and lack of access to the markets hindered climate action. The main practices by farmers were crop diversification (79%), soil-water conservation (66%), use of organic fertilisers (78%), and management of residues (69%). The novelty of the study is that it summarises perception, adaptation and mitigation into one analytical model, which exposes the behavioural interrelationships that constitute resilience. The results also highlight the effectiveness of enhancing social learning in networks, financial, and mainstream climate-smart agriculture in supporting low-carbon adaptive food systems in semi-arid areas of South Asia.

title: Rethinking the Psychoanalysis of Masculinity
abstract: Drawing on a broad range of psychoanalytic, cultural and social influences, the author examines the concept of toxic masculinity for how it brings into focus a widespread anxiety about toxicity throughout daily life: In nature, society and personal relationships. Aggressive, misogynistic masculinity has become a major topic in recent years, spreading throughout popular culture, the media and research. Often called 'phallic,' it simmers in everyday life and hits the headlines for turning florid and violent in maintaining its dominance, especially towards women. But at the extreme, phallic masculinity has recently crystallized in a very different form, as toxic masculinity, and 'toxic' has become the near-universal epithet for all forms of extreme destructiveness in a 'toxic culture.' It has brought into focus, and named as masculine, an anxiety over toxicity in every corner of everyday life. Exploring toxic masculinity in depth brings out a misogynistic current that pervades individual and social realms, but also throws a sharp light on normal masculinity. By elaborating on the roots of this toxicity, Figlio is able to draw out a different, more positive alternative for masculinity, with particular reference to the underlying fears around fertility and the seminal. With a strong research and clinical base, this book is essential reading for all psychoanalysts and psychoanalytic psychotherapists and cultural and social theorists interested in exploring concepts of masculinity.

title: Autism Disease: Neural Network Going Awry and Therapeutic Strategy Underlying Neural Plasticity
abstract: Autism is the major form of Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD). Autism was first discovered in 1940s and has attracted enormous research and social activities recently. It is a disease currently defined only by behavior problems including impairments in communication, inability in social interactions, and stereotyped patterns of interest and behavior. Because of the complexity nature of the disease, there are many basic questions yet to be answered by scientific research. Autism is of great and increasing public health concern because the number of children receiving services is growing each year. In this commentary review, we will analyze recent studies on brain structure, genetics, and brain conditions and graph an overview of autism from these findings. Under the basis of synaptic plasticity, we believe the findings have led us to propose a hypothesis on therapeutic strategy, by which we may be able reshape the troubled neural network towards its normal networking function. [N A J Med Sci. 2011;4(3):139-150.]

title: Prevalance of Alcohol Abuse in Calabar South Local Government Areas Cross River State
abstract: This study examined the prevalence of alcohol abuse in Calabar South, Local Government Area of Cross River State, Nigeria. Unlike earlier studies of alcohol use in Nigeria, the study focused on a segment of the population that is difficult to reach and probably at high risk of alcohol and drug abuse. In addition, the focus of this study was on both western and the traditional alcohol beverages. The sample consisted of 400 respondents aged 10-50 years resident in Calabar South. Life time consumption of alcohol was reported by 98.5% of the respondents. Beer was the most often consume alcoholic drinks in the study population by the male while wine was for female, 64% of males took beer while 36% of females took wine. the odds of taking alcoholic drink increased with age. The consumption of alcohol was described as very harmful to health by 48% of the sample Analysis of the data showed that the factors that mostly influenced alcohol drinking were its availability which stood at 52.75%, peer groups influenced 27.25%, mass media advent 7.5%, home 9.5% and school 3.0%. The study also showed that alcohol consumption had effect on the social behaviour of the people of Calabar South. Decreased work performance 77.25%, increase in violence and crime 77%, poverty 50.75%, wife and childbearing 73.75%, increase in accident rate 80.5%, children inability to continue schooling 83.5% Nigerian culture, it appears that there is a culture of alcohol implicitly institutionalized that one could easily brand it as a norm to drink alcohol across the whole social spectrum with the student population constituting a significant proportion of the risk group (Ifeagwazi,2007).

title: Farmers’ experiences with extension services in promoting sustainable land use practices in Fanteakwa South municipality
abstract: This study explored farmers’ experiences with agricultural extension services in promoting sustainable land use practices in the Fanteakwa South Municipality of Ghana. Guided by participatory extension, social learning, innovation diffusion, and systems theory, the research adopted a qualitative exploratory case study design. Data were collected through focus group discussions with twenty farmers and key informant interviews with extension officers, farmer-based organizations, traditional leaders, and other stakeholders. Thematic analysis revealed that farmers accessed extension messages through group meetings, community information centers, radio programs, and home visits. While farmers expressed general satisfaction with these methods, they highlighted differing preferences based on accessibility and interaction, with farm visits and group methods valued for their practical and interactive nature. Extension agents promoted practices such as soil fertility management, agroforestry, crop rotation, erosion control, and water conservation. Adoption, however, was constrained by financial limitations, lack of access to credit, and the technical complexity of extension messages. Facilitators included trust in extension officers, peer learning, and practical demonstrations. The findings underscore the need for farmer-centered extension approaches that integrate financial support mechanisms, participatory learning, and coordinated stakeholder engagement to enhance adoption and ensure the sustainability of land use practices in farming communities. title: Stigma and support: Infertility’s varied face across urban and rural India
abstract: Introduction Infertility remains a significant, often stigmatized condition affecting many women worldwide. In India, the prevalence of primary infertility ranges from 3.9% to 16.8%1, presenting unique challenges within its diverse sociocultural landscape. Despite advancements in medical science, the journey of women grappling with infertility is profoundly shaped by societal norms, cultural expectations, and varying levels of access to health care. This commentary delves into the sociocultural dimensions of infertility in urban and rural India, reflecting on a recent study that elucidates these complexities and underscores the need for tailored interventions. Infertility as a sociocultural phenomenon Infertility transcends its physiological implications, embedding itself deeply into the emotional and psychological fabric of affected individuals. Parenthood in India is not merely a personal milestone but a societal expectation reinforced through social learning. The desire to have children is often intensified by cultural narratives that celebrate parenthood as a pinnacle of personal achievement and social duty2. In urban settings, the pressures of infertility manifest differently compared with rural areas. Urban women often face a dual burden: the societal expectation to conceive and the demands of a fast-paced, career-oriented lifestyle. Higher education and professional aspirations can delay marriage and childbearing, inadvertently increasing the risk of infertility. The recent study highlighted that urban women, who were generally older and more educated than their rural counterparts, experienced greater psychological distress with higher psychological evaluation test scores. Conversely, rural women navigate infertility within a framework of traditional beliefs and limited health care access. Infertility is frequently perceived as divine retribution or a familial curse, exacerbating the social stigma and psychological burden. The study found that rural participants faced more significant social isolation and lacked spousal and familial support, contributing to heightened emotional distress. The urban-rural divide The dichotomy between urban and rural experiences of infertility in India is stark. Urban areas, with their greater access to medical facilities and diverse perspectives through globalization and media, offer different coping mechanisms and support systems3. Women in urban settings are more likely to seek assistance from fertility clinics and support groups. However, the pressures of balancing career pursuits with family expectations can intensify stress, as evidenced by the higher psychological evaluation test scores among urban participants. In contrast, rural communities are characterized by traditional beliefs, limited health care access, and stronger adherence to cultural norms that prioritize childbearing within marriage. The study highlighted that rural participants, despite being younger on average, faced more significant challenges due to these entrenched beliefs and a lack of resources. The reliance on supernatural explanations and remedies for infertility further complicates the psychological landscape for rural women. Sociocultural pressures and psychological distress Both urban and rural women in India face intense sociocultural pressures regarding conception, albeit in different forms. Urban women contend with societal expectations to balance professional success with family life, leading to significant stress. The study found that urban women experienced major stressors related to societal expectations, contributing to their higher psychological distress4. Rural women, however, deal with the immediate and pervasive expectations of their communities and extended families. The pressure to conceive soon after marriage is particularly pronounced in rural areas, where traditional values sway. This pressure is compounded by social isolation and a lack of support from spouses and families, as noted in the study. The emotional toll of these expectations can be profound, leading to feelings of inadequacy and heightened psychological distress. The role of education and access to health care Education and access to health care emerge as critical factors influencing the experience of infertility. The study revealed that urban participants, with higher levels of education, were more likely to delay marriage and childbearing, increasing the risk of infertility. However, their education also provided them with better access to medical information and health care services, including fertility treatments5. In rural areas, limited education and health care access present significant barriers. The study noted that a significant proportion of rural participants were illiterate or had only primary education, which restricted their understanding of infertility and available treatments. The lack of accessible health care facilities further exacerbated the challenges, leaving many rural women without adequate medical support. Financial constraints and infertility treatments The financial burden of infertility treatments is a significant stressor for women in both urban and rural settings. The high costs of fertility treatments can lead to increased stress and treatment dropouts, particularly among urban participants, who face the economic demands of continuous treatments6. The study underscored the need for affordable treatment facilities and financial support to alleviate this burden. In rural areas, financial constraints are compounded by the lack of proper information and access to allopathic treatments. Many rural women rely on traditional remedies or seek supernatural healing due to the unaffordability and unavailability of modern medical treatments. The study emphasized the importance of enhancing health care infrastructure and education in rural settings to address these barriers. Tailored interventions and future directions The findings of the study underscore the necessity for tailored interventions that address the diverse needs of urban and rural women dealing with infertility. Culturally sensitive support systems are crucial in providing the emotional and psychological support needed to navigate the complex journey of infertility. In urban areas, interventions should focus on balancing career aspirations with family expectations, providing mental health support to manage stress, and facilitating access to fertility treatments. Support groups and counseling services can play a vital role in mitigating psychological distress. In rural settings, enhancing health care infrastructure and providing comprehensive reproductive health education are essential. Community-based interventions that involve family members and address traditional beliefs can help reduce the stigma associated with infertility. Financial support and affordable treatment options are also critical to ensuring that rural women have access to necessary medical care. Conclusion Infertility is a multifaceted issue that requires a nuanced understanding of the sociocultural dynamics at play. The recent study provides valuable insights into the differing experiences of urban and rural women in India, highlighting the need for targeted interventions. By addressing the unique challenges faced by these women, we can work towards alleviating the psychological burden of infertility and supporting women in their journey towards parenthood. Further research is needed to deepen our understanding of the sociocultural factors influencing infertility and to develop effective strategies for intervention. Conflict of interest disclosures The authors declare that they have no financial conflict of interest with regard to the content of this report.

title: Introduction: The Genesis of Mother — Infant Interaction: How Parents Create Persons
Comment on “Level the Playing Field to Bolster the Boardroom: Sports as a Springboard for Women's Labor Force Advancement in A sia”
abstract: Kotschwar and Stahler's (2016) paper can be divided into two parts. The first part compares the global position of Asian women in education, labor force, and corporate leadership bodies. The second part advocates promoting Asian women in sports and presents research on the long-term economic benefits that participation in sports can provide women internationally, including labor force participation and enhanced returns to education and labor outcomes. Kotschwar and Stahler then propose sports program-related policies for Asian countries so as to better integrate Asian women into education, society, labor, and corporate boardrooms. Gender equity is part of the growing academic and policy interest on inclusive growth that includes education and employment opportunities. Gender equity can be measured by economic-social indicators of access to resources and outcomes – in family and societal status, in education and health, and in employment opportunities and corporate and government leadership. Kotschwar and Stahler's unique contribution is the advocacy of sports participation to achieve gender equity. What is the evidence on Asian female participation in education, employment, and leadership roles? Indicators show that Asian females still lag males with variations according to subregion and indicators. The gender gap in years of schooling has narrowed considerably, but not gender gap on tertiary education specialization in sciences and engineering. Further, Asian female participation lags in occupations such as legislators, senior officials, and managers and corporate leadership. Explanations across economies and societies include stage of economic development, female educational opportunities, and social-cultural norms affecting education and labor participation and opportunities up the corporate ladder. A fundamental factor is women's conflicting dual role in the workplace and home and motherhood (particularly in urban settings). This dual role is deterring, depending on: social-cultural norms and policies affecting the type of jobs suitable for females, re-entry into the labor force of married women after completing their childcare responsibilities, availability of alternative childcare and homecare arrangements, and impact of pro-family public policies and services. In promoting female higher education and labor force participation, policy-makers in countries experiencing severe fertility decline have to recognize that fertility rates are going to drop further. There is ample evidence that as educational and labor market opportunities for women increase, their opportunity cost of child-rearing also rises. Additionally, Kotschwar and Stahler's hallmarks of success for women have excluded their critical role of nurturing the moral, social, and intellectual development of the next generation. What are the benefits of gender equity in participation in education, employment, and leadership roles? First, in Asian economies facing aging and declining populations and labor shortages, increased female participation (in addition to increased male and elderly participation and inflows of foreign labor) will alleviate labor shortages and enhance economic growth prospects. Second, gender diversity in boardrooms would improve corporate performance, particularly as females are major decision-makers regarding household expenditures. Third, for families, improved education for females improves quality of home care and child care and labor force participation contributes to family income and financial security. Fourth, at the individual level, education and employment satisfy personal aspirations, improve social status and social interaction, increase opportunities for meaningful and remunerative employment, and provide financial security. Females form half the human race and their personal well-being is as important as for males. Kotschwar and Stahler recognize that promoting sports participation is only one way of achieving gender equality. Is it the best way given limited time and financial resources? Kotschwar and Stahler highlighted particularly positive social and personal attributes of female athletes. More robust evidence on Asia is needed to support their argument that sports provide girls with the following positive attributes better than alternative activities – ability to compete, be a team player, to win and lose with grace; female athletes have a better chance of graduating high school and college; girls’ participation in high school sports linked to positive effects on achievement in science; sports lead to higher paying careers; strong association between sports participation and corporate leadership. Sporting programs, facilities, and finance should be equally accessible to males and females as part of the overall program of pursuing gender equity. But why single out sports? If the issue is only gender equity and improving the lot of females, will efforts to improve the workplace for females, such as flexible employment and removing impediments to re-entry into the labor market after their child-caring years, improve female labor participation? Will careers uninterrupted by marriage and motherhood remove employer biases against corporate training of female executives and facilitate their climb up the corporate ladder into senior managerial positions and the boardroom? Will changes in societal attitudes toward gender demarcation of work and responsibilities remove gender inequality? Top sportswomen can act as role models for other girls, but so can excellence in other activities. Moreover, sports as a remunerative career is elitist, has a very limited life span and can benefit only a limited number of individuals, whether male or female.

title: A Study to Assess the Effectiveness of Planned Teaching Programme on Knowledge regarding Optimal use of Antibiotics to prevent Bacterial Resistance among Mothers at Selected Community Area, Kollam
abstract: The present study entitled “A study to assess the effectiveness of planned teaching programme on knowledge regarding optimal use of antibiotic to prevent bacterial resistance among the mothers at selected community area, Kollam’’ was undertaken for partial fulfillment of degree of B. Sc. nursing at Bishop Benziger College of Nursing, Kollam which is affiliated to Kerala university of health sciences during the year 2017–2018. The objectives of the study were to assess the pretest knowledge regarding optimal use of antibiotics to prevent bacterial resistance among the samples, to determine the effect of planned teaching program on knowledge regarding optimal use of antibiotics to prevent bacterial resistance, to find the association between pretest knowledge and selected demographic variables. An experimental approach was used for this study. The sample comprised of 60 mothers residing in selected community area, Kollam. The tools used for data collection were structured knowledge questionnaire and planned teaching programme for assessing pretest and posttest knowledge. The collected data were analyzed by using descriptive and inferential statistics. The result showed that majority of samples (45%) belonged to the age group in between 20–30 years, (25%) were in the age group in between 31–40 years, (15%) were in the age group below 20 years and (15%) were in the age group above 40 years. Most of the samples among the mothers (98%) were Christians and (1.66%) were Muslims. The samples among the mothers participated in this study (51.60%) belonged to nuclear family, (40%) belonged to joint family and (8.33%) belonged to one parent family. Most of the samples are among the mothers of children below 15 years, (60%) have two children, (30%) have one child and (10%) have more than two children. The samples among the mothers participated in this study have educational status of SSLC and below SSLC (65%), (28.33%) of them have educational status of degree, (5%) are pre degree and (1.66%) is in other category. Most of the mothers of children below 15 years have monthly income between Rs.2000–5000 (66.66%) and (33.33%) are in between Rs. 5001-10000. Most of the samples participated in this study use television (65%), (16.66%) uses newspaper and magazines, (3.33%) of them use radio and (15%) of them uses all above accessible mass medias. After the planned teaching program, the result of posttest shows that most of the samples (76.66%) attained excellent knowledge, (21.66%) got good knowledge, (1.66%) got average knowledge. It was analyzed that there is significant in posttest knowledge scores. So the planned teaching program of our study was effective. It was computed to determine the association between level of knowledge and selected demographic variables and it showed that age, religion, type of family, number of children, education status, monthly income, accessible mass media had no significant association with knowledge.

title: Fetal Alcohol Syndrome
abstract: Objectives After completing this article, readers should be able to:Alcohol is the most common human teratogen, but its significant physical and neurobehavioral effects are completely preventable. Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) was described initially in case reports by Lemoine in 1968 and Jones and Smith in 1973. It is a pattern of physical, behavioral, and cognitive abnormalities seen in individuals exposed to alcohol in utero. The association between these findings and maternal use of alcohol during pregnancy has been well documented, with studies in both animals and humans suggesting teratogenicity from as little as one binge drinking episode in early pregnancy. The diagnostic criteria are not a result of fetal physical dependence or addiction or the presence of alcohol in the neonate at delivery; rather, they are teratogenic effects caused by in utero exposure to alcohol in the mother’s blood. In 1996, following a congressional mandate that the Institute of Medicine and National Academy of Sciences study FAS and related birth defects, these institutions published a review of the current understanding of FAS and revised the diagnostic criteria. Despite increased awareness of this preventable birth defect,new cases continue to occur in significant numbers and are routinely under-recognized by medical personnel. It is imperative that maternal alcohol use and its sequelae be considered and addressed in daily pediatric practice. The purpose of this article is to review the diagnosis, epidemiology, management, prognosis, and prevention of FAS.FAS represents a specific pattern of findings associated with in utero exposure to alcohol(Table 1). These include: pre- and postnatal growth deficiency, minor facial anomalies(short palpebral fissures, ptosis, flat midface with upturned nose, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip), and central nervous system (CNS) neurodevelopmental findings(microcephaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, tremors, hyperactivity, learning disabilities, cognitive impairments). Infants exposed to alcohol in utero also can have major malformations, including cardiac defects, cleft lip, cleft palate, and limb reduction deformities.Using the criteria established by the Institute of Medicine, the diagnosis of FAS requires a history of maternal alcohol use during the pregnancy (proven or presumed) and elements of the three primary diagnostic categories (Table 2). If maternal alcohol use is not confirmed, the diagnosis of FAS may still be used, but the missing history of in utero alcohol exposure should be noted. Fetal alcohol effects are minor findings that are not necessarily unique to alcohol,but that are proven to occur in association with in utero alcohol exposure. However, this term is imprecise. The Institute of Medicine uses the terms partial FAS with confirmed maternal alcohol exposure, alcohol-related birth defects (ARBD), and alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder (ARND) to describe alcohol-related effects not meeting the criteria for FAS.The incidence of FAS, ARBD, and ARND has been difficult to characterize because of significant variations in study populations and methods of data collection. Prospective studies and newborn discharge diagnosis data give lower incidence rates; retrospective studies and clinic-based studies tend to report higher incidence rates. The reported ranges of FAS, ARBD, and ARND are generally between 0.5 and 5 per 1,000 children, making alcohol exposure the most common cause of birth defects.Significant controversy surrounds the amount of alcohol ingestion that presents a risk to the fetus and whether a single exposure is of greater consequence than a pattern of exposure during fetal development. Initial studies of human alcohol teratogenicity examined the average amount of alcohol consumed per day during pregnancy. These studies did not demonstrate a difference between infants exposed to higher levels of alcohol or to binge drinking. However, the definitions of binge drinking were vague,and neurobehavioral and longitudinal effects were not addressed. This approach also failed to distinguish between infrequent binge drinkers who may have occasional high blood alcohol levels and mild-to-moderate regular drinkers who have lower peak blood alcohol levels but a more continuous fetal exposure.Subsequent animal studies have helped define the specific gestational timing and doses of alcohol needed to produce both structural and behavioral teratogenic effects. Specifically, animal studies suggest that: 1)third trimester alcohol exposure decreases brain weight and numbers of neurons, 2) peak blood alcohol concentration (affected by both dose and rate of consumption) is more critical than the same total dose with lower peak blood alcohol concentration, and 3)exposure early in the pregnancy can produce more severe and more consistent effects. An absolute threshold and critical time period for exposure is suspected, but has yet to be demonstrated.If this information is extrapolated to human alcohol teratogenicity, one can predict potential fetal effects from a single binge episode (five or more drinks in one sitting) during early development. However, the effects of low total alcohol consumption in a pattern that avoids high peak blood alcohol concentrations (ie, one to two drinks per week with no binge episodes) are unknown at this time. The prevalence of maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy increased from 12.4% to 16.3% between 1991 and 1995. Frequent drinking during pregnancy, defined as more than seven drinks per week, increased from 0.8% to 3.5%. In the face of increasing maternal alcohol consumption,researchers still cannot define the threshold for alcohol toxicity in the fetus.Developing organisms are uniquely susceptible to external teratogenic influences. The clinical findings in FAS result from exposure of the developing fetus to toxic levels of alcohol and its metabolites at critical periods in development. The specific pathophysiology remains unknown, but may involve free radical formation that causes cellular damage in the developing tissues of the fetus. Exposure in the first trimester affects organogenesis and craniofacial development, leading to minor and major malformations, such as the characteristic facial features and ARBD (Table 1). Excessive cell death in the midline of the developing embryo may account for the development of these facial features. Continuing alcohol use by the mother in later pregnancy causes decreased fetal growth that results in low birthweight and affects postnatal growth. Alcohol use most likely affects CNS development throughout the pregnancy, as the brain is forming early in the first trimester and is undergoing a growth spurt with maturation of the neurons in the second and third trimesters. Thus,alcohol exposure at varying times in pregnancy can cause similar CNS neurodevelopmental effects.Alcohol use also affects fetal nutrition. Obviously,alcoholism may affect maternal dietary habits and health maintenance behaviors. In addition, alcohol affects the maternal metabolism of essential nutrients by decreasing intestinal absorption, increasing renal and hepatic metabolism, and decreasing placental uptake and availability to the fetus.Finally, the use of other drugs (marijuana, nicotine,caffeine) that commonly accompanies alcohol consumption can have detrimental effects on the fetus. Clear delineation of alcohol-related effects is difficult in many situations where polysubstance use is present.Differences in the severity and spectrum of FAS have been observed based on genetic background, but it is unclear whether confounding variables may have affected the data. For example, population-based studies document up to 10-fold higher prevalence rates of FAS among Native American tribes than in the overall American population. However, individual tribes have markedly differing prevalence rates of FAS. This may be due to confounding factors in the population-based approach, such as counting each sibling of an affected family as a separate case. If a family that included six affected children was counted as six individual cases, the local prevalence of FAS would be higher than if the same family was counted as a single case (one mother delivering multiple children who had FAS). The two methods of interpreting the data would result in different conclusions about the prevalence of FAS within a small, closely related community, resulting in different genetic implications. One of the issues under investigation is the possible genetic susceptibility within the Native American population to the teratogenic affects of alcohol. Further work is necessary to establish the cause of the varying prevalence rates.The concordance of FAS is higher in monozygotic twins than in dizygotic twins, supporting the concept of genetic factors in the fetal effects of alcohol. Mouse embryo studies show variation in CNS injury when the same dose of alcohol is given to different strains of mice,further demonstrating the variation in phenotype based on genetic background.One possible mechanism of heritable susceptibility to FAS may be genetically encoded differences in alcohol dehydrogenase, the enzyme responsible for metabolizing alcohol in the liver. In mothers of children who have FAS, the enzyme may be less functional, resulting in higher peak blood alcohol concentrations after the ingestion of alcohol. Alternatively, the fetus may be deficient in alcohol dehydrogenase activity and, thus,less able to tolerate elevated maternal alcohol levels. Clearly, the effect of genetic variation on susceptibility to in utero alcohol toxicity is an area for future research.Alcohol exposure can continue postnatally if the infant is breastfeeding. Alcohol is excreted in human milk at concentrations similar to blood levels, but acetaldehyde,an alcohol metabolite that may act as a teratogen, is not excreted into human milk. Although the resulting serum alcohol level in the infant may be low, the combined effect of alcohol on the physiologic and social aspects of the breastfeeding relationship are significant. Three points are of particular concern. First, infants’nursing behavior and total consumption of milk are adversely affected by maternal alcohol use immediately prior to a feeding. Second, suckling-induced prolactin and oxytocin release are inhibited by alcohol. Third,infants born to alcohol-abusing mothers have poor suck patterns and do not feed well at the breast. These findings are of significance to the nutritional and emotional aspects of the mother-infant relationship.FAS is a clinical diagnosis assigned in the setting of maternal alcohol use. The typical pattern of associated features should trigger an investigation into possible fetal alcohol exposure and evaluation for other aspects of the syndrome. In many situations, the diagnosis will not be clear, requiring further evaluation by clinical geneticists and neurodevelopmental specialists, with chromosomal analysis for other causes of facial dysmorphology and neurodevelopmental abnormalities.Neonatal diagnosis usually depends on characteristic facial features, suspected in utero alcohol exposure, low birthweight, poor growth, and microcephaly (Tables 1 and 3). The combination of congenital malformations and poor growth should prompt an investigation into prenatal alcohol exposure. The neonate who has FAS may manifest CNS signs, such as irritability and hypersensitivity,hypotonia, poor feeding, and difficulty bonding with caregivers. Congenital malformations and CNS signs are nonspecific, however; facial features are the most useful criteria in the newborn and infant.The diagnosis of FAS is easier between ages 2 and 11 years, when the facial features are still prominent and typical CNS dysfunction emerges clinically. As the child approaches school age, the behavioral and cognitive aspects of the syndrome may become more pronounced, often causing difficulty with developmental tasks. From school entry through adolescence, these aspects can affect school performance and social interactions with peers. Cognitive manifestations, such as memory deficits and slow information processing, are reflected in intelligence quotient (IQ) testing. Typical FAS neurobehavioral and adaptive manifestations in the school-age child include attention deficit disorder (which may be unresponsive to stimulant medication),impulsiveness, extreme mood changes, anxiety, aggressive behavior, resistance to change, frequent temper tantrums,and difficulties with social peer interactions. In addition, these children may have speech impairment as a result of anatomic differences of the jaw, fine motor dysfunction of the oropharyngeal muscles, or hearing deficits. Cognitive and behavioral difficulties also affect communication skills. A recent study estimated that the social abilities of a child who has FAS plateau at the 6-year-old level and may not progress beyond this point (see Thomas et al in Suggested Reading). The authors also showed that the interpersonal relationship skills of children who had FAS were below the level of verbal IQ-matched controls. It is easy to see how these issues will affect social interactions and classroom skills negatively. Diagnosis in the school-age child can be made clinically if the facial features are classic, CNS abnormalities are present, and maternal alcohol use during pregnancy is established. Chromosomal analysis,genetic evaluation, and neurodevelopmental evaluation are important in confirming the diagnosis. As a child ages, the facial features (especially the smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and flat midface) may become harder to distinguish, making clinical diagnosis more difficult (Figs. 1 and 2). “Catch-up” growth may occur in adolescence, particularly in females. The CNS manifestations of the syndrome and the resulting impact on cognitive skills become more prominent in adolescence. Problem-solving abilities, abstract reasoning, and time and money management skills are deficient. These teenagers can be impulsive, use poor judgment, and fail to understand the consequences of their actions. In adulthood, these individuals can be isolated and withdrawn, with poor adaptive living skills. Some are unable to work or manage money and often require structured living arrangements. Cognitive abilities vary considerably within the group of children affected with FAS. Some can function successfully in a regular classroom and attain meaningful employment and even college. More severely affected children may have significant developmental delay and learning disabilities that require special programming at school and lifelong supportive services. IQ scores of children who have FAS range from 16 to 105, with an average of 66. In comparison, IQ scores of male patients who have fragile X syndrome range from 30 to 55, and those of children who have Down syndrome range from 25 to 50, with only a few testing in the 60s. FAS is among the most common causes of mental retardation, but as demonstrated by the average score, most children have only mild retardation (IQ scores below 70 are consistent with mental retardation). Even children who have FAS and normal IQ scores may have significant neurobehavioral deficits and adaptive problems that affect their independence, and they are at higher risk for severe behavioral problems and psychiatric disorders. Approximately 62% of patients who have FAS have severe behavioral problems compared with 15% to 32% of those who have Down syndrome. Individuals who have FAS may face more difficulties holding a job, maintaining social relationships, and living independently than people who have Down syndrome and similar or even lower IQs.For example, consider John, a 7-year-old boy who was exposed to alcohol in utero and has facial features consistent with FAS, height at the 10th percentile,weight less than the 5th percentile, and head circumference less than the 5th percentile for age. FAS was diagnosed clinically in his first year of life based on the in utero alcohol exposure, growth retardation,microcephaly, and facial features in conjunction with a negative evaluation for genetic and other known disorders. His home environment was evaluated, support services were arranged for his mother, and evaluation for alcohol-related disability was arranged for his older sister. John’s IQ is 75. Speech delay affects his school performance and social interactions. He is having increasing difficulties with attention during the school day, aggressiveness toward peers, mood swings, and temper tantrums. These further impair his school performance and peer interactions. John also has specific difficulties with math and organizational skills. He will require evaluation for supportive behavioral and educational services, despite his normal IQ, and for hearing impairment and will need close monitoring for other problems that may develop in the future.Other social and pathologic processes affect children who are exposed to alcohol in utero. Labeling affected children as having ARND may overlook additional negative influences on their cognition and behavior. For example,many children who have FAS and ARND also live with poverty, unstable home situations, lack of emotional support systems, and inappropriate educational resources. These situations can cause fear, depression, and frustration that may be misinterpreted as alcohol-related behavioral problems. It can be easy to blame all of a child’s difficulties on prenatal alcohol exposure,when part of the problem may be ongoing exposure to external influences.The differential diagnosis of FAS is important because the FAS phenotype is variable and may be difficult to distinguish from other conditions. The physical features can be confused with those of Aarskog syndrome, Williams syndrome, Noonan syndrome, Dubowitz syndrome, Bloom syndrome, fetal hydantoin syndrome, and maternal phenylketonuria fetal effects (Table 4). The neurobehavioral features may be similar to those seen in fragile X syndrome, the 22q11 deletion syndromes, Turner syndrome, or Opitz syndrome (Table 5). When contemplating the diagnosis of FAS, it is important to consider these and other genetic, metabolic,toxicologic, and neurodevelopmental syndromes and to seek consultation as necessary.The early diagnosis of FAS benefits infants and children. Medical intervention, including evaluation of growth and nutrition, management of medical issues related to birth defects, and identification of other medical issues specific to the child in question, is crucial to the care of the child who has FAS. Other appropriate interventions, in the form of educational evaluation and support and community resources, can be accessed and put into place early, allowing the child to reach his or her maximum potential.
