title: An interview with Dr Fuller Warren Bazer
abstract: Fuller W. Bazer is a reproductive biologist. His research and other scholarly activities focus on uterine biology and pregnancy. He has made significant contributions to understanding mechanisms of action of pregnancy recognition signals from the conceptus to the maternal uterus, including discoveries of interferon tau (IFNT) and estrogen from ruminant and pig conceptuses, respectively. The roles of components of uterine secretions, including glucose, fructose, amino acids, transport proteins, regulatory molecules, growth factors, and enzymes and endocrine regulation of their secretion is another major research interest with respect to the growth and development of the conceptus (embryo/fetus and placenta). Dr Bazer’s research has also explored the mechanism(s) of action and potential therapeutic value of conceptus interferons and uterine-derived hematopoietic growth factors, particularly uteroferrin, in both pigs and sheep as models for human disease. I received my B.S. in Biology from the Centenary College of Louisiana with initial interests in going to medical school, but I became more interested in veterinary medicine. Texas A&M University (TAMU) accepted seven students from Louisiana into each of their classes in the College of Veterinary Medicine, but they required that applicants should have several courses in animal sciences. I went to Louisiana State University (LSU) in the Fall of 1960 to take the perquisite courses. One of those courses was reproductive physiology and that subject became of great interest, because I could see not only the link between reproduction and reproductive health in animals and the need to provide high-quality animal protein but also the issues of fertility and reproductive health in humans. I went on to get my M.S. in Animal Science from LSU in January 1963 and then began my required service as an active duty soldier. I served as an Army Air Defense Officer at Fort Bliss, Texas, and in South Korea. While on duty in South Korea, I thought a lot about whether to go to graduate school or professional school to become a veterinarian. Because of my research experience at the LSU, I chose to go to graduate school at the North Carolina State University beginning in August 1965. My Ph.D. was awarded in January 1969, but I had already begun my career in the Department of Animal Science at the University of Florida (UF) in October 1968. So, my interest in reproductive physiology was because of my interest in the subject and my appreciation of the need for research into issues of reproductive health and fertility in both humans and animals. My path to becoming a scientist began at the LSU as I learned the scientific method and began to design and conduct research for the M.S. degree. That continued at the North Carolina State University as I conducted research, taught laboratories, and mentored undergraduate students during my Ph.D. program. During my Ph.D. program, I hypothesized that there was, in the uterine milieu, a hormone like ecdysone in insects. Ecdysone is required for larvae to undergo pupation. At about that time, Dr Joseph Daniel’s laboratory described blastokinin (also known as uteroglobin), which was claimed to be required for morulae to transition to blastocysts. I wondered if blastokinin might be the mammalian equivalent of ecdysone. I became very interested in molecules in the uterine lumen that might influence the growth and development of the conceptus, and my initial research at the UF involved analyses of uterine flushings on specific days of the estrous cycle and pregnancy. The first protein of major interest discovered in my laboratory was a purple protein that became known later as uteroferrin. The next focus of my research was on pregnancy recognition signaling molecules from the conceptus, which led to the discovery in my laboratory of estrogen as the signal in pigs and IFNT as the signal in ruminants. Those areas of research were the focus in my laboratory, but in due course, there were shared interests leading to collaborative research with Drs. Donald Barron, Bill Thatcher, Dan Sharp, Don Caton, Bob Abrams, and Michael Roberts, which greatly contributed to my development as a scientist. Later, at TAMU, collaborations with Drs. Guoyao Wu, Bob Burghardt, Greg Johnson, Tom Spencer, Troy Ott, Xiaoqiu Wang, and Laurie Jaeger contributed very significantly to my scientific career. Dr Mary Warters, Head of Biology, Centenary College of Louisiana, was the first scientist to stimulate my interests in the field of biology, including embryology, physiology, and comparative anatomy. Then, Dr Stewart Fowler at the LSU taught me reproductive physiology and pointed me in the direction of my career in that field of study. At North Carolina State University, Dr Lester Ulberg and Albert Clawson were my mentors, and Dr Sam Tove was a great instructor from whom I learned to appreciate biochemistry. Although it was these faculty members who influenced my career path, it was my father, Raymond Bazer, who told me I needed to go to college at least for 1 year to see where that would lead, and he told me that an education is something no one can ever take away from you. Later, he and my mother wanted to know—“son when will you be finishing your education.” They were both from a time and place where a sixth grade education was considered enough since working on the farm or elsewhere to help support family was their destiny. The first major decision, after deciding on my career tract at the LSU, was the decision to go to the North Carolina State University for my Ph.D. The second major decision was to accept the position at the UF, where I was able to enjoy working with so many others, some of whom were colleagues, and some of them are both colleagues and friends. The tough decision to leave the UF and move to TAMU was a good one as I had been at UF for 24 plus years. The change in culture and collaborators at TAMU were very stimulating as there were new opportunities to pursue and more friends and colleagues with whom to collaborate. I learned about this new Society for the Study of Reproduction (SSR) when I was a graduate student at North Carolina State University and wanted to join as soon as it formed. But my mentors were very much entrenched in the American Society of Animal Science and were certain SSR would not succeed, so I was discouraged from joining SSR at its beginning. Nonetheless, after taking my faculty position at UF, I became a member of SSR in 1969. The goal of SSR to bring together scientists from health science centers, departments of biology, and departments of animal sciences to share the latest research and foster collaboration at the most basic level through to translational and applied research was most appealing to me. The breadth and depth of the science presented at SSR kept me abreast of the frontiers in reproductive biology and had a great impact on my thinking. It helped me formulate good questions and hypotheses as well as methods to test those hypotheses. It is fair to say that the SSR has been vital to any successes I have enjoyed during my 52 years in academia. First, there was the discovery of uteroferrin and it roles in transplacental transport of iron via the areolae on the placenta and in stimulating hematopoiesis. Second, there was the discovery that estrogen is the pregnancy recognition signal in pigs by altering secretion of prostaglandin F2α (PGF) from an endocrine direction (cyclic pigs) to an exocrine direction (pregnant pigs) [1–4]. Bill Thatcher and I next designed experiments to determine if estrogen was involved in pregnancy recognition signaling by sheep and cow conceptuses. It was not, so we turned to studies using radiolabeled amino acids and conceptus cultures to discover what is now known as IFNT. This led to a large research effort that led to the understanding that IFNT silenced the expression of receptors for estradiol and oxytocin to prevent the uterus from releasing oxytocin-dependent luteolytic pulses of PGF (Figure 1). At Texas A&M, we discovered that IFNT silences the expression of all classical interferon-stimulated genes in uterine luminal and superficial glandular epithelial cells, but in concert with progesterone, increases the expression of a variety of genes critical for growth and development of the conceptus. Among those genes are those for the transport of nutrients, such as arginine, leucine, glutamine, and glucose, which support the development and survival of the conceptus. This link between nutrients and reproduction in pigs and sheep is a third major area of research in my laboratory in collaboration with Drs. Guoyao Wu and Greg Johnson after my move to the Texas A&M [5–9]. Interferon tau (IFNT) is the pregnancy recognition hormone in sheep and other ruminants that acts to silence expression of estrogen receptor alpha (ESR1) and, in turn, oxytocin receptor (OXTR) to prevent development of the luteolytic mechanism that required oxytocin (OXT) from the corpus luteum (CL) and posterior pituitary to induce luteolytic pulses of prostaglandin F2α (PGF). (Used with permission from 1). The students I have accepted in my lab typically contacted me directly and expressed their knowledge of and interest in published work from the lab. Students are mentored so that they understand that training begins with a task, but learning begins with a question. This is important because successful graduate students must be able to both formulate sound hypotheses and apply appropriate techniques to test those hypotheses. The value of teamwork is also emphasized because working with large animals requires a team and conversations among members of the team enhance learning. I also remind graduate students that they volunteered to enter graduate school and that if they are not excited about their choice, they need to identify an alternative to graduate school. I always encourage social interactions among graduate students and faculty, which build comradery and provide a relaxed environment to brainstorm new ideas and share advice and experiences, which are all essential to a successful graduate training. Finally, I always endeavored to transmit these lessons through my own actions. I never asked a graduate student to do other than what I was willing to do myself. There are a couple of pitfalls that need to be avoided. First, beginning graduate students need a project that is within their capabilities and will yield useful results. More senior graduate students are expected to build from this and engage in projects with higher risks but are potentially transformative to the discipline. It is also important that a student understands and takes ownership of their project and that the project can be completed in a reasonable period of time. I have seen some graduate students be assigned a project that is beyond their capabilities, and this is a major pitfall. I am probably not alone among scientists in considering gene editing technology to be a tremendous breakthrough in science. The ability to insert, delete, and modify genes to understand their function is, and will continue to be, transformative to biology and is key to understanding those genes most critical to the establishment and maintenance of pregnancy. Cryopreservation of gonadal tissue from which viable gametes can be recovered and be used to establish successful pregnancies is another breakthrough. This technology will greatly benefit human medicine, animal agriculture and endangered species conservation as individuals with conditions known to compromise fertility can retain the option of successfully producing offspring. That is a difficult question to answer. I am concerned that the National Institutes of Health (NIH) is demanding that funded research be almost immediately relevant to human health, so it is difficult to get funding for basic research with animal models other than rodents. That was not true in 1968 when I began my career. Also, funding from the USDA is very limited for research in reproductive biology. This is surprising, since a safe, abundant, nutritious, and affordable supply of high-quality animal protein is essential to health, and reproductive health is essential to propagation of all species. Stated more simply, humans must eat and reproduce to maintain the health and viability of families, communities, nations, and humanity. I recommend that young scientists think about the following points as they develop strategies to be productive in scholarly activities that impact the discipline of reproductive biology: Challenges: Limitations on funding competitive grants jeopardize research for both production agriculture and biomedical research. There is a lack of advocacy for use of livestock models for biomedical research even in the face of extensive evidence of the value of these models to human health. Scientists on grant review panels and funding administrators are often unfamiliar with livestock as animal models. In some institutions there is a “cultural” notion that biomedical research with livestock is inappropriate to the Land Grant mission, but they fail to understand that biological systems are common across all animals, so what we learn from one species can be applicable to improving reproductive health and fertility in other species. Agricultural colleges are often separated from human and veterinary medicine and other life sciences disciplines, which creates a “silo” effect that detracts from the recruitment of researchers who will be competitive for extramural funding. How to overcome these challenges: Seek employment at institutions that provide incentives for animal scientists to collaborate broadly, establish interdisciplinary perspectives, and interject novel insights into traditional programs. Increase awareness that isolation of agricultural research is no longer viable as state and federal support for agricultural research declines. Be proactive in strengthening collaborations among animal scientists, biomedical researchers, and basic science departments. Support advocates that strive to prioritize research at the NIH that benefits both animal agriculture and human medicine. Champion administrators with skills and vision to foster interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary research. Seek to increase representation of animal scientists on NIH Study Sections and advocate for USDA to significantly increase funding for animal agriculture. Recognize and use state-of-the art technologies for research, which advances the understanding of key mechanisms at the most basic molecular and cellular levels, which impact reproductive performance and fertility. Here are some guidelines that are useful: learn to say “no” and focus on a few goals and projects that allow for adequate family time; have family dinners and conversations daily; have a “date night” with your spouse each week; and respect the needs of spouse and children. I believe that the NIH must reassess its current funding priorities and place greater value on funding research with livestock. Given that most assisted reproductive technologies, as well as knowledge of most aspects of reproductive biology, are founded in research conducted using livestock species, future advances will be limited unless they change. The USDA must garner greater advocacy for competitive funding for high quality research. That change must be strongly supported by the leadership at the Land Grant universities and commodity groups. It is unfortunate that more than a decade after USDA launched its Agriculture and Food Research Initiative (AFRI), it is yet to be funded by the congress at its authorized appropriation of $700 M. In 2019, the appropriation was barely 60% of this amount. If the funding does not increase, the economic viability, sustainability, and competitiveness of animal agriculture will be compromised.

title: Biochar for sustainable agricultural intensification: technical/economic potential, and technology adoption - eScholarship
abstract: Growing population, changing climate, and human development will require sustainable agricultural intensification in sub-Saharan Africa -- a region where most people still live in rural areas, and rural poverty remains severe. While the 20th century saw massive increases in agricultural productivity over most of the world, sub-Saharan Africa was largely bypassed. In many respects, catching up in the 21st century poses more difficult challenges than were faced in the 20th -- with the novel challenges of climate change, soil degradation, and the closing agricultural frontier being chief among them. Solutions are required that profitably improve productivity, strengthen and/or rebuild soil fertility, and do so within the limits imposed by a warming and carbon-constrained world. This will be needed if the region is to shake off the stagnation that has characterized it for the past century, and contribute to solving to the global challenges posed by the coming century.This dissertation focuses on one potential solution -- biochar -- and follows it from agronomic efficacy, to preliminary economic analysis, to rigorous trial in the field. As such, it seeks to be an example of the interdisciplinary approach that I argue is needed to guide the development, deployment, and scaling of solutions to problems in the environment/development space.The first chapter is a meta-analysis of crop yield response to biochar. Using data from 84 studies, I (and co-authors) employ meta-analytical, missing data, and semiparametric statistical methods to explain heterogeneity in crop yield responses across different soils, biochars, and agricultural management factors, and then estimate potential changes in yield across different soil environments globally. We find that soil cation exchange capacity and organic carbon were strong predictors of yield response, with low cation exchange and low carbon associated with positive response. We also find that yield response increases over time since initial application, compared to non-biochar controls. High reported soil clay content and low soil pH were weaker predictors of higher yield response. No biochar parameters in our dataset -- biochar pH, percentage carbon content, or temperature of pyrolysis -- were significant predictors of yield impacts. Projecting our fitted model onto a global soil database, we find the largest potential increases in areas with highly weathered soils, such as those characterizing much of the humid tropics. Richer soils characterizing much of the world's important agricultural areas appear to be less likely to benefit from biochar.The second chapter is a preliminary economic analysis of biochar's potential in two contexts -- rural western Kenya, and northern Vietnam. Using recall-based datasets from smallholder farmers, I (and co-authors) estimate yields as a function of biochar and fertilizer use. We find an positive association between biochar use and average yields in Kenya, but no correlation in Vietnam. We then use these estimates to calculate optimal input mixes under hypothetical biochar and carbon prices, given heterogeneity in response both to biochar and fertilizer, and heterogeneous budget constraints. In Kenya, we find that biochar is more-likely-than-not to be profitable to adopt for 23\% of our sample if unsubsidized and available at its current sale price of around \$188/ton, while a hypothetical carbon subsidy of \$100/ton CO$_2$e increases this proportion to 47\%, though these proportions are not different from zero at 95\% confidence. Because of limited short-term complementarity between biochar and inorganic fertilizer, we estimate that biochar adoption would change profits little, given budget constraints for agricultural inputs. We conclude that carbon subsidies may have a marginal impact on biochar's profitability in Western Kenya, but that further research is needed to improve the precision of these estimates, extend them to account for any longer-term changes in soil characteristics that might impact biochar's profitability, and account for any potential biases stemming from time-varying variables that not measured or modeled in the context of this study.The third chapter reports the results of a Kenyan field experiment on adoption and impact of biochar, which was motivated by the encouraging findings of the previous two studies. In addition to technical efficacy, I sought to determine what mix of policies might most effectively speed biochar dissemination, given the slow pace of technological change in African agriculture over the past several decades. I randomly assigned prices, demonstrations, and risk-free trials. Yields increased by 37\% and 50\% in the first two seasons, and response to inorganic fertilizer improved. However, uptake was 2.6\% and 10\% respectively. Farmers were highly price-sensitive. Social network effects were marginally significant, but positive at low penetration and negative at high penetration. Given uptake well below the social optimum, subsidies for biochar appear justified from a social cost/benefit standpoint. The dissertation closes with a short discussion of lessons learned, and ways forward for further applied research.

title: POSTER SESSION III SATURDAY, OCTOBER 4, 2003 7:45 AM–10:00 AM
abstract: * SEVERITY OF PEDIATRIC CROHN'S DISEASE DURING FIRST YEAR OF FOLLOW-UP: AN ANALYSIS OF THE PREDICTIVE VALUE OF BASELINE VARIABLES. J Critch, P Kundhal, C Smith, M Zachos, A M Griffiths, The Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto, ON, Canada; Janeway Hospital, St. John's, NL, Canada The variable natural history of Crohn's disease (CD) makes initial treatment selection difficult. If traditional “step-up” treatment paradigms are to be replaced with early introduction of immunomodulatory and biologic agents, it is important to identify subgroups of patients likely to have a more severe clinical course. We undertook to prospectively identify baseline factors predictive of severity during the first year following diagnosis of pediatric CD. Patients aged <17 years were enrolled in the study at the time of diagnosis of CD at The Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto from July 1997 – May 2001. The primary outcome variable was disease severity during the subsequent year as measured at one year by Physicians Global Assessment using a 4-point categorization scale used in previous research (quiescent, mild symptoms only, exacerbations but remissions, chronically active) (Griffiths, Gut 1993). Construct validity testing of this outcome measure was performed in the current study using prospectively accrued hospitalization data, PCDAI scores, linear growth and disease-specific quality of life assessment. The influence of baseline variables (age, gender, disease location, lab tests, initial therapy, PCDAI scores) and early treatment response (complete vs. partial/none) on one-year disease severity was determined by multivariate analysis. 122 patients (64% males) with mean age at diagnosis 13.1+/−2.4 years were included in the study. Macroscopic disease involved colon only (26%), small bowel only (23%), small bowel and colon (51%). In one-year follow-up 73 (60%) experienced quiescent/mild disease and 49 (40%) moderate/severe disease. Univariate analysis demonstrated worse disease severity was associated with low albumin (p=0.004), high PCDAI (p<0.001), initial hospitalization (p=0.004), initial corticosteroids use (p=0.003) and incomplete response to initial therapy (p=0.014). In multivariate regression analysis, PCDAI score was the only independent predictor of subsequent disease severity (OR 1.057; 95%CI 1.025-1.090). Disease activity at diagnosis is predictive of disease severity during the first year in pediatric-onset CD, but much variability remains unexplained. These data support targeting patients with higher disease activity for early immunomodulatory therapy. INCREASED PREVALENCE OF COLONIC-PREDOMINANT DISEASE PHENOTYPE IN EARLY ONSET INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE. Melvin B Heyman, Barbara S Kirschner, Benjamin D Gold, George Ferry, Robert Baldassano, Stanley A Cohen, Harland S Winter, Terry Smith, Hashem B El-Serag, the Pediatric IBD Consortium, University of California, San Francisco; University of Chicago; Emory University, Atlanta; Baylor College of Medicine, Houston; Children's Hospital of Philadelphia; MassGen Hospital, Boston Up to 25% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) report symptom onset before 18 years of age. Limited data exist that characterize the population-based epidemiology and phenotype of IBD in very young patients. We sought to describe epidemiological features at initial presentation of pediatric IBD in the United States. A registry was developed to uniformly collect data from a cohort of IBD patients enrolled between January 2000 and November 2002 at six pediatric centers (Pediatric IBD Consortium). All patients had IBD diagnosed before 18 years of age. 1,370 pediatric patients were entered in the registry. The mean age of IBD diagnosis was 10.3±4.4 years; 46% were female and 85% Caucasian. IBD diagnosis was confirmed in 83 (6.4%) in the first two years of life, and in 211 (15.4%) before 6 years of age. 654 (47.7%) were diagnosed between 6 and 12 years, and 505 (36.9%) were diagnosed between 13 and 18 years. The proportion of newly diagnosed patients with colitis (UC or IC) declined in older children. Over 63% of the patients <8 y/o were diagnosed with UC or IC (disease limited to the colon), whereas only 35% of those =8 y/o had colonic-only disease (p <0.0001). Positive family history of IBD was present in 3% of siblings and 29% of all extended family members. The prevalence of first-degree relatives affected with IBD was greatest in the subgroup of children diagnosed with UC =2 years of age (44%). IBD is frequently diagnosed in young children and infants in this cohort of children from 6 geographically different centers. While isolated colitis (UC and IC) and CD are equally distributed in young children, CD predominates in older children with IBD. Family history of IBD is observed in 29% of our cohort and is especially common in younger patients with UC. Early onset IBD with a colon-predominant disease phenotype may represent a patient population in which to identify genetic risk factors or environmental triggers for IBD. Supported in part by grants from the CCFA, NIH DK61617, and VA HSR&D CDA. PERMANENT GROWTH FAILURE (GF) IN PEDIATRIC CROHN'S DISEASE (CD). Elizaveta Iofel, Kathleen Grancher, James Markowitz, Jeremiah J Levine, North Shore -LIJ Health System, New Hyde Park, NY Data from children treated in 1970s-1980s demonstrate frequent stunting in young adults diagnosed with CD before puberty. Given recent changes in CD therapy, we sought to determine the frequency of permanent GF in young adults diagnosed with childhood onset CD over the past 2 decades. AIM: 1) To evaluate final adult height (FAH) of children diagnosed with CD during early puberty. 2) To identify therapies associated with decreasing risk of stunting. Charts of 78 consecutive patients with CD treated after 1988 were reviewed. Subjects were excluded if they were Tanner stage (T) ≥3 at diagnosis (dx), <T5 at the last visit, were treated with growth hormone, or if insufficient growth records were available. GF at diagnosis was defined as height ≥2 major growth channels below preillness height percentile. Permanent GF was defined as 1) FAH ≥5 cm less than predicted based on midparental height or 2) FAH percentile ≥ 2 major growth channels below preillness height percentile. 40 patients (29M; age at dx 11.2 ±2.7 yrs, age at FAH 20±1.9 yrs) satisfied study criteria. FAH percentile distribution was as follows: TABLETableWhile parental heights showed no predisposition to short stature, the distribution of FAH in subjects was shifted towards the lowest percentiles. 18 of 40 patients (45%) were found to have permanent GF. Nine of 40 patients (23%) had FAH at <5% range. No difference was observed in corticosteroid, 6MP, or nutritional supplement use between the subjects with or without GF. None of 6 patients who underwent surgery at T1-3 developed GF, in contrast 4 out of 6 patients who had surgery at T 4-5 had GF (p<0.05). Twelve of 32 patients (38%) with available growth records had growth delay at the time of dx. Of these 12, six (50%) developed permanent GF. Of 20 patients with normal growth at dx, 9 (45%) developed permanent stunting. 1) Among young adults with CD diagnosed before pubertal growth spurt, the distribution of FAH percentiles is markedly shifted toward the lowest percentiles. 2) Normal growth at dx is not predictive of the normal FAH. 3) Ileocolonic resection done during T 1-3 appears to protect against GF, and may be more effective than nutritional supplementation or the use of 6 MP. COMPARISON OF DUAL ENERGY X-RAY ABSORPTIOMETRY AND QUANTITATIVE CALCANEAL ULTRASOUND IN THE EVALUATION OF BONE MASS IN PEDIATRIC INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE. Manisha Harpavat, David J Keljo, A'Delbert Bowen, Susan L Greenspan, Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA; University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, PA Decreased bone mineral density (BMD) and increased fracture risk have been reported in children with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD). The gold standard for determining BMD is Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA). DXA involves radiation and uses a two dimensional technique to calculate density. Quantitative ultrasound (QUS) provides a radiation-free assessment of bone density and quality. The purpose of this study was to compare DXA measurements of the total body, hip, and spine to QUS measurements obtained from the calcaneus. Nineteen otherwise healthy children newly diagnosed with IBD, who were within three weeks of initiation of therapy, underwent DXA and QUS measurements. Bone mineral content (BMC, grams) and BMD (grams/cm2) of the whole body, hip (femoral neck and trochanter) and lumbar spine were assessed by DXA (Lunar DPX-L). Broadband ultrasound attenuation (BUA; dB/MHz) was measured in the posterior part of the calcaneus by QUS (Quidel QUS-2). Of the 19 newly diagnosed children, 14 had Crohn's disease (CD), 4 had ulcerative colitis (UC) and 1 had indeterminate colitis. Mean age was 12 yr (range of 7.4-16.7). Correlation coefficients between DXA and QUS ranged from 0.42-0.72. Positive significant correlations were found between calcaneal BUA and whole body (BMC and BMD), femoral neck (BMC and BMD), trochanter (BMC), and lumbar spine (BMC and BMD) (Table 1). These results indicate that QUS measurements of the calcaneus positively correlate with DXA measurements of the whole body, femoral neck, and lumbar spine. Calcaneal QUS may be useful for screening children newly diagnosed with IBD for decreased BMD.Table 1: Spearman rank-order correlation between DXA and calcaneal BUA measurements ALTERED BONE MINERAL DENSITY IN CHILDREN AT TIME OF DIAGNOSIS OF INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE. Manisha Harpavat, Susan L Greenspan, A'Delbert Bowen, David J Keljo, Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA; University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, PA Osteoporosis has been found in children with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD). Steroid use is often implicated as the major risk factor for reduced bone mineral density (BMD). The role factors such as nutrition, steroids, or disease activity contribute to osteoporosis remains unclear. The purpose of this study was to measure the BMD of a cohort of children newly diagnosed with IBD and to examine factors associated with abnormalities in BMD. Nineteen otherwise healthy steroid naive children who were within 3 weeks of initiation of therapy, underwent Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA; Lunar DPX-L). BMD measurements were reported as Z scores, the number of standard deviations (SD) the patient's BMD is from the mean BMD expected for the patient's peers matched for age, gender, and race. Since children with IBD can have a delay in bone age, an x-ray of the left wrist was obtained for bone age determination. Z scores were recalculated after BMD measurements were normalized to each child's bone age. Correlation between specific disease variables and BMD was examined. Among the 19 children, 14 had Crohn's disease (CD), 4 had ulcerative colitis (UC) and 1 had indeterminate colitis. Mean age was 12 yr (range 7.4-16.7). Four of 19 patients (21%) had total body BMD Z scores of < −1 SD, with 3 patients having low bone mass (Z score between −1 SD and −2 SD) and 1 patient having very low bone mass (Z score < −2 SD). Ten of 19 patients (53%) had lumbar spine BMD Z scores of < −1 SD, with 8 patients having low bone mass and 2 patients having very low bone mass. IBD patients had significantly reduced mean lumbar spine BMD Z scores (p=0.008). No correlation was found between BMD Z scores and ESR, albumin, or PCDAI for the CD patients. IBD patients had significantly lower weight (p=0.001) and BMI (p=0.001) values than expected for age. Decreased BMD is common in children newly diagnosed with IBD. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine BMD prior to initiation of steroid therapy. Lumbar spine, made of metabolically active trabecular bone, is particularly affected. Nutritional status as reflected by weight and BMI, is significantly impaired. In this cohort of patients, it will be important to evaluate the effects of nutrition, disease activity, and steroids on bone metabolism. DISCORDANCE BETWEEN ERYTHROCYTE SEDIMENTATION RATE AND C-REACTIVE PROTEIN IN PATIENTS WITH INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE TAKING AZATHIOPRINE OR 6-MERCAPTOPURINE. Barrett H Barnes, Stephen M Borowitz, Martha A Hellems, Frank T Saulsbury, James L Sutphen, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA The course of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is characterized by periods of relapse and remission. Treatment is aimed at reducing symptoms during relapses and prolonging time in remission. 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) and its pro-drug azathioprine (AZA) are commonly used to prolong remission. The Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) are widely used laboratory markers of inflammation. We have observed discordance between ESR and CRP in a number of children with IBD treated with AZA or 6-MP. The purpose of this report is to characterize children with IBD treated with 6-MP or AZA who remain in remission and have a persistently elevated ESR in the face of a normal CRP. Patients seen in the Pediatric Gastroenterology Clinic between 1/1/1995 and 12/31/2002 with a principal diagnosis of Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis treated with AZA or 6-MP continuously for at least four months were identified and their medical records reviewed. 120 patients met eligibility criteria. 12 had persistently elevated ESR in the face of a normal CRP without signs or symptoms of active disease when the ESR was elevated. Duration of disease and duration of 6-MP or AZA were somewhat greater in children with discordant ESR and CRP than in children where ESR and CRP were comparable (70.4 ± 21.8 vs. 54.3 ± 40.1 mos., p=0.045 and 59.7 ± 16.6 vs. 36.6 ± 24.1 mos., p=0.002). There were no differences between the groups in any other clinical feature examined (diagnosis, location of disease, age at onset of symptoms) nor were there any differences between the groups in any laboratory values examined (HCT, MCV, WBC, serum albumin, serum total protein level, estimated serum globulin levels). Many clinicians use ESR as an indirect means of assessing intestinal inflammation in childhood IBD. Our results suggest among children treated with AZA or 6-MP, CRP may be a more reliable indicator of intestinal inflammation. While we do not know the mechanism, certain children taking AZA or 6-MP may have persistent elevations of the ESR in the face of a normal CRP and no clinical evidence of active IBD. CROSS-CULTURAL ADAPTATION OF THE PEDIATRIC INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE QUESTIONNAIRE (PEDIBDQ): DEVELOPMENT OF A US SPANISH VERSION. Multicenter studies require availability of culturally adapted versions of outcome measures. Our goal was to adapt the PEDIBDQ, a disease-specific HRQL instrument, for US Spanish-speaking children with IBD. title: تدوین اصول طراحی محلهی دوستدار کودک با رویکرد تقویت حس اجتماعی کودکان (نمونهی موردی: محلهی رشدیه تبریز)
abstract: Introduction Children, as a significant part of the urban population, play a major role in the use of urban spaces. Nowadays, paying attention to this part of society has been considered by urban planners and stakeholders since the number of children in urban areas of the world is growing (Kiani and Esmailzadeh, 2012: 51). Children in urban areas have problems such as lack of safe, creative, and lively spaces, environmental pollution, high density of buildings, and lack of security and clearance. Besides, due to lifestyle changes in recent decades, children often live in small residential units, and have no option for entertainment except watching television, playing computer games, playing with siblings or neighbors’ children, and sometimes reading books in the dark or noisy space of the building (Shia, 1391: 44). These issues reduce the presence of children in the urban spaces, leading to serious damage in their growth and social development. Based on a common and widespread belief, the child is defined as a member of society who still does not have an effective role in social organization due to not being equipped with the social skills (Kermani and Ebrahimabadi, 2014: 7). Children have four growth dimensions: physical development, emotional development, cognitive development and social development (Nowruz and Nastaran quoted by Rice, 2014: 5). This study tried to deal more accurately with the issue of children's social development in urban spaces in the neighborhood scale along with the importance of other aspects of children's development. The neighborhood is the first scale of public space in which children experience life and extend their learnings to larger urban environments. Social development is related to the process of socializing a child for communicating with others, from family members to friends and peers. The presence of children in the public environment can have further benefits such as social understanding, the sense of trust, and mutual support (Tranter and Pawson, 2001). In the first step, this research tried to compile a guide for the design or renewal of neighborhoods that "social sense" can be promoted. Therefore, the main question of the research was: "Which characteristics of a neighborhood can promote the children's social sense?" In the second step, a neighborhood in Tabriz city (Rushdiyeh neighborhood) was selected to examine that guide. The current study aimed to develop a guide for designing child-friendly urban neighborhoods focusing on the sense of community development. Research methodology The methodology of this research, which was based on the paradigm of realism, deals with the objective characteristics of the environment to advance the goals of the research. Regarding the qualitative research method, questionnaire techniques, interviews (individual and group), and cognitive maps were used to extract more information. The statistical population included preschool children (5-7) and primary school children (7-12) and their parents in Rushdiyeh neighborhood. A total of 60 children and 25 parents were surveyed as a statistical sample from the neighborhood. The method of collecting information is documentary and field. In order to know the case sample, first, the required maps were prepared based on the subject and after a complete knowledge of the range, the case sample was analyzed. Then, based on the research problem and the points we obtained from the theoretical foundations, the knowledge and analysis of the scope, design, and presentation of the proposal was done. Finally, based on the findings and theoretical framework of the research, an urban design guideline was developed to strengthen the sense of community of children in the neighborhood. Discussion According to the theoretical foundations and studies of child development and child-friendly city, the concept of sense of community and the development of this concept for children, we summarized, concluded, and developed a framework for designing a child-friendly neighborhood based on the sense of community; We also tried to answer the research questions by recognizing and analyzing the case study. In the context of the child-friendly city, more has been done to meet the basic needs and rights of children and to keep their social and emotional development low. In modern cities, it has caused less interaction between residents and people by eliminating or reducing public spaces, and this in itself has reduced the sense of community among communities, which also applies to children. Children need to be part of the group and influence this group and establish a common emotional bond with them and try to meet the needs of the group. If they can experience social sense during this period, they will build a better society in the future, which will lower social norms in the future and strengthen the social and emotional development of children. In today's modern cities, children have little presence and interaction in the neighborhood and urban space, which in turn causes psychological and social harm to children, which may lead to various anomalies in the city community in the future. Children currently have to be with their parents to attend the neighborhood or city, and this allows parents to accompany their children only on holidays due to their busy schedules, and on other days of the week, children are either at home or in kindergarten. Also, they spend the day at school and have fewer games and social interactions at the neighborhood and city level. In this regard, the following fifteen principles were argued to create a child-friendly neighborhood for the development of the sense of community: Principle 1: In designing neighborhood spaces, informal spaces for the presence of children (alleys, streets, etc.) are as important as the designed formal spaces (for example, play spaces in parks). Principle 2: The design should be based on passive supervision to ensure the safety of children when in public. Principle 3: Children use the potential of any activity to engage in social interactions, so it is important to pay attention to all three types of activity (necessary, social, and selective). Principle 4: Public walkways in the neighborhood should be designed based on speed C (traffic calming) to provide the necessary safety for the presence of children. Principle 5: Designing special traffic lines that end in primary schools provides sufficient security for children to have personal access to school. Principle 6: Public spaces, especially alleys, provide physical flexibility for a variety of children's play. Principle 7: Children's play spaces should be combined with other spaces such as the elderly to sit to improve social sense by understanding other cycles of life. Principle 8: Design of retail activities in the special movement paths of children to schools. Principle 9: Combining children's spaces with green spaces. Principle 10: Design a neighborhood based on specific (implicit or obvious) edges to better understand boundaries. Principle 11: The existence of spaces in which children can interact with children in other neighborhoods through play. Principle 12: Designing a neighborhood center based on the scale of the child and the presence of the child in it as one of the basic neighborhoods for socialization. Principle 13: The existence of institutions such as libraries and cultural centers with appropriate functions for children in the neighborhood. Principle 14: Climatically protected play spaces for attendance at different times of the year. Principle 15: Organizational management of the neighborhood for greater participation of children in the neighborhood and matters related to their management. On the other hand, assuming the desired principles and based on different dimensions of child development, it is possible to provide a suitable urban design guide for the child-friendly neighborhood. Based on the fifteen principles and also the design guide, the necessary arrangements regarding Rushdiyeh neighborhood are as follows: 1. Creating a sidewalk and bicycle path for children on the way to school; 2. Equipping parks and green spaces to create official play spaces and their appropriate distribution in the neighborhood, as well as creating new parks such as adventure and intellectual parks; 3. Creating an excuse for children to be together, such as a wall for children to paint; 4. Planting plants in places built by children; 5. Creating a library for children; 6. Creating sports and cultural spaces; 7. Creating sports fields for group sports; 8. Placing urban furniture for children in spaces; 9. Adaptation of public spaces for the presence of children in them; 10. Increasing the education per capita in the area; 11. Locating small businesses near and along the school route.

title: Evidence for improved outcome for children born with a univentricular heart defect?
abstract: Children who are born with a congenital heart defect (CHD) requiring open-heart surgery have an excellent survival rate. Thus, more attention is drawn on the neurodevelopmental outcome and quality of life of these survivors. The reason for this is 2-fold: first, we need to obtain outcome information in order to provide information for parents, health professionals and insurance companies on the spectrum, severity and prevalence of potentially occurring impairments. This enables an early implementation of therapeutic intervention and by that an improved outcome. Secondly, outcome assessment is a critical quality control tool that allows for the identification of modifiable risk factors in the treatment phase of these patients. So far, the majority of studies reporting neurodevelopmental outcome focused on early childhood and early school age. There, a variety of developmental impairments have been described, ranging from motor coordination disorders [ 1 ] visuomotor problems [ 2 ] to language delay and overall intellectual impairments [ 3 ]. The literature on the late school age and adolescent outcome is limited. There is evidence that motor difficulties may persist into adolescence [ 4 ]. Furthermore, studies have described behavioural deficits such as hyperactivity and attention problems [ 5 ], which are reported to occur in 5 and 41% of children operated for CHD. There is also evidence for a coexistence of both motor and behavioural difficulties [ 1 ]. The overall intellectual outcome for adolescents with transposition of the great arteries lies within the normal range [ 6 ]. One could argue that a normal overall IQ should be sufficient for a good school performance and academic achievement. However, another intellectual domain, that is ‘executive function’, plays a critical role in a child's cognitive functioning, behaviour, social interactions and academic achievement, independent of the overall IQ. Executive functions are a set of higher-order self-regulatory and control mechanisms that include various cognitive processes, such as inhibitory and interference control, working memory, cognitive flexibility, verbal fluency and planning. Efficient executive functions are critical for a child's cognitive functioning and academic achievement and deficits in executive functions have been frequently described in children who were born very preterm and recently also in adolescents with CHD [ 6 ]. Children with a univentricular heart defect (UVH) seem to have the poorest neurodevelopmental outcomes, partly because of the combination of a variety of risk factors for poor outcome (for review see Ref. [ 7 ]). Recently, early childhood cognitive outcome for children with UVH was described to be rather favourable with a mean mental developmental index within the normal range [ 8 , 9 ]. However, early outcome findings have limited predictive value for school outcomes. The study by Sarrechia et al. [ 10 ] in this issue of EJCTS examines this important open question. They evaluated 17 UVH patients in comparison with 46 children with surgically corrected biventricular CHD (for atrial or ventricular septal defect). At 9 years of age, children were examined with a wide range of standardized tests to assess cognitive, behavioural and executive functions. Children with UVH showed normal mean IQs (mean IQ: 101, range: 73–130). This seems promising and should be regarded as a very favourable outcome. However, the authors also report that almost half (47%) of the parents of children with UVH reported school problems such as repeating a grade or receiving special education compared with 11.8% in control parents. These findings are in line with the reported problems in attention and executive functioning, memory and sensorimotor functioning as well as in visuospatial processing. Unfortunately, there is no information on the proportion of children who performed below one standard deviation of the mean IQ of the test norms (100) or of the controls (107.8). This proportion may be higher than the norm despite a mean IQ that lies within the normal range due to skewing of the IQ distribution curve towards the left. This phenomenon has been described in other at-risk populations such as children born preterm. The study by Sarrechia et al. [ 10 ] reveals a few methodological problems that need to be pointed out and taken into account when concluding that outcome is very favourable for survivors with UVH. First, the included number of children is small ( n = 17) and does not allow for the identification of risk factors for poor outcome. Secondly, the authors excluded all children with genetic abnormalities, developmental syndromes and cerebral palsy. By doing so, the most adverse outcomes were excluded. While many studies exclude patients with genetic abnormalities, the exclusion of the two other developmental impairments, albeit understandable in the view of planned neuropsychological testing, may lead to a distortion of the actual outcome as these impairments may potentially be associated with the underlying CHD or a consequence of it. As we do not know how many children belonged in these categories, we cannot draw any conclusion on the full spectrum of outcomes. Thirdly, the follow-up rate of 59 percent is rather low and leaves us to speculate about the neurodevelopmental status of the remaining 41%. They may be similar to the examined group, but may represent a more severely affected or a less severely affected subgroup. In addition, there is a lack of neuroimaging data, which would allow correlating functional with structural findings [ 4 ]. The above-mentioned limitations are clearly acknowledged by the authors and lead to the following conclusion: Because of the small number of patients with complex CHD treated in each single centre, it is mandatory to conduct multicentre studies or registries to obtain outcome information on a large enough sample, which will help to disentangle the complex interaction between disease severity, co-occurring medical and patient-inherent risk factors, environmental factors and pre-existing changes in brain development and their effect on long-term neurocognitive outcome. One first step in this direction has been achieved by the International Cardiac Collaborative on Neurodevelopment in which outcome results of over 1700 CHD patients were pooled (Ganyor et al. Pediatrics, In press).

title: Something from Nothing:
abstract: At the opening of Chaucer's early dream vision, the Book of the Duchess, the narrator describes his insomnia and his general idle malaise: I have so many an ydel thoghtPurely for defaute of slepThat, by my trouthe, I take no kepOf nothing, how hyt cometh or gooth,Ne me nys nothyng leef nor looth.All is ylyche good to me—Joye or sorowe, wherso hyt be—For I have felyng in nothyng.(4–11)1 The relentless negations in these lines—denials of action, thought, being, and feeling—emphasize the narrator's lack of productive intellectual or social influence and his emotional void. Yet “nothing” takes on an allegorical force as it “cometh or gooth” and as the narrator describes his “felyng in nothyng.” This allegory illogically suggests that the Dreamer finds something—a feeling—in nothing, a paradoxical notion that anticipates a deep preoccupation throughout the poem with a making something from nothing, valuing passive as active, and finding productivity in idleness.2Idleness is an important though little-studied aspect of medieval culture, as James Simpson has argued.3 Simpson articulates a literary principle of “idling” based on the repeated echoing of prior sources. In doing so, he suggests, a poem “enacts yet somehow resists the possibility of literary waste; it recycles even as it appears to waste.”4 In her book on medieval gossip, Susan Phillips takes up the issue of idleness much more extensively, making a case for the productive capacity of idle talk.5 Like both of these scholars, I am interested in idleness and its productive potential. I will integrate and expand on their work by approaching the subject of idleness with a particular focus on gender and sexuality. In doing so, I hope to illuminate a queer dimension to the notion of productive idleness by articulating a poetics of idling in Chaucer's first dream vision.The apparent passivity of the melancholic narrator has been a focus for many scholarly treatments of the poem influenced by queer theory and gender studies.6 Most notably, for my purposes, Steven Kruger argues that the Dreamer's melancholia at the beginning of the poem works as a queering force, rendering him passive and effeminate. Kruger further suggests that it is through the Dreamer's homosocial interaction with the Black Knight within his dream that his melancholic state is corrected.7 While such treatments of the poem are valuable, I wonder why we must locate the poem's queer dynamic within a gender inversion, insisting on the equation of a male character's “passivity” with “femininity.” I would like to move beyond this correlation by suggesting that neither “femininity” nor “queerness” must be passive. The Dreamer and the Black Knight mobilize their unproductive physical and mental states—their idleness—toward emotional and creative production. Instead of “being idle,” they are “idling.” This active participial form inscribes a measure of activity into the apparent stagnancy of their idleness.The Book of the Duchess emphasizes idleness at three levels. First, Chaucer thematizes it by highlighting how the Dreamer's melancholia prevents him from writing poetry, rendering his languor akin to a particularly humanist brand of melancholy: accedia, or intellectual and creative torpor. Yet at the end of the poem, as the Dreamer returns to his pen, prompted by his marvelous dream, the melancholic state that has produced his dream is reinscribed as productive. In the figure of the Black Knight, the Dreamer's idleness is extended and magnified, as the Knight's despair at the loss of his wife approaches a kind of spiritual sloth, or acedia. The Dreamer's intervention into the Black Knight's melancholy introduces another idle mode in the poem—one that emerges at the level of narrative and discourse. As R. A. Shoaf has demonstrated, the Dreamer acts as a kind of secular confessor to the Black Knight, probing him about his dead lover in a strategy that resembles the questions of a priest taking confession.8 However, several scholars have pointed out that the intimate personal detail required for confession renders it dangerously close to that most maligned form of “idle talk”—gossip.9 At the same time that the Dreamer acts as a secular confessor to the Black Knight, their conversation also resembles gossip. Yet their idle talk is not passive or unproductive. The confessional, gabby, discursive resonances of the men's verbal exchange elevate the intimacy between the Dreamer and the Black Knight, allowing for the partial consolation of an intimate or queer friendship. This dynamic undermines Kruger's point that their homosocial interaction acts as a corrective force.10 Finally, Chaucer's poetics of idling emerges at the level of poetic form, as the poem ends by rearticulating its own origin. Despite this regressive movement, which imitates an idle mechanism in its deceptive lack of progression or movement forward, the poem gestures outward to Chaucer's future poetic corpus in a way that renders the poem's idle circular structure an active force.The Book of the Duchess offers an early example in an English literary tradition of texts that depict men being idle in an intimate or homoerotic way.11 Such an association highlights the lack of social productivity—and biological reproductivity—in queer relationships, a point that has recently become the focus of a particular strand of queer theory espoused by Lee Edelman and others, known as the “antisocial thesis.”12 Edelman points to the violence of “reproductive futurism,” that is, the social and political emphasis on reproduction, the child, and the future.13 In making this important claim, Edelman nihilistically identifies the “death drive” as a queer imperative. In contrast, I would like to show how the queer friendship in the Book of the Duchess is invested, in its emotional and poetic productivity, in the future. My reading renders queer idleness an active, productive force, and so aligns with queer theorists like Eve Sedgwick, who sees queer as “a continuing moment, movement, motive—recurrent, eddying, troublant.”14 The Book of the Duchess is doubly queer as the intimacy cultivated between men is heightened and as the poem renders idleness into idling—an irrepressible cycle of production.The Book of the Duchess's focus on illness and grief highlights both the Dreamer's and the Black Knight's idle or unproductive conditions and enables their conversation to function as recuperative idle talk. The Dreamer's complicated gender is evident from the outset of the poem, as are the physical and spiritual conditions that inform his dream. Chaucer's narrator emphasizes the Dreamer's physical and psychological infirmity, telling us, “I may nat slepe wel nygh noght;/I have so many an ydel thoght” (3–4). He stresses his overactive imagination, asserting that his dazed languor is a result of “sorwful ymagynacioun” (14) and specifying that he suffers from “melancolye” (23). Moreover, the narrator's illness renders him “a mased thyng” (12), passive and impotent. The narrator tells us that his sickness and insomnia are “agaynes kynde” (16), a phrase that, as Kruger points out, would strongly resonate with moralizing rhetoric focused on sexual behavior contra naturam.15The nuance contained in the notion of the “ydel thoghts” that the Dreamer identifies in line 4 is worth examining in greater detail. The word idel and its variants in Middle English carry associations of laziness, worthlessness, emptiness, and lack of productivity.16 The Dreamer's idle thoughts underscore his overactive imagination. This emphasis on idleness hints at the nature of the Dreamer's melancholic condition. The word suggests that the Dreamer has no outlet for his lively fantasies. His transgression is not the medieval sin of acedia, a temptation that incites flight from spiritual exercises and ultimately produces alienation from God and despair. This spiritual condition emerges later when the Black Knight's malady begins to resemble religious despondency. Instead, the Dreamer's melancholy bears a likeness to the more broadly philosophical Petrarchan concept of accidia: the melancholic inhibition of creative production brought on by despair in the human condition.17 Furthermore, Middle English notions of idleness shifted semantically between intellectual production and biological reproduction. In his Confessio Amantis, for example, John Gower uses the word to refer to fallow land: “And ek the lond is so honeste/That it is plentevous and plein,/Ther is non ydel ground in vein” (7.930–32).18 Though many of the references to idleness denoting physical reproduction refer to land, the word's association with stopped or blocked fertility gives us greater insight into the nature of the Dreamer's ailment. Combining with his melancholic physicality, the Dreamer's idleness separates him from the imperative norm of production.19The Black Knight's depleted vitality echoes that of the Dreamer. Reflecting the narrator's assertion that he is “Alway in poynt to falle a-doun” (13), the Black Knight feels “Hys sorwful hert gan faste faynte” (488). Chaucer zeroes in with minute precision on the physiology of the Knight's swoon: The blood was fled for pure dredeDoun to hys herte, to make hym warm—For wel hyt feled the herte had harm—To wite eke why hyt was adradBy kynde, and for to make hyt glad,For hyt ys membre principalOf the body; and that made alHys hewe chaunge and wexe greneAnd pale, for ther noo blood ys seneIn no maner lym of hys.(490–99) Chaucer's detailed attention to the internal flux of the Black Knight's body reinforces the moist humoral associations accompanying melancholia and ties his experience to the Dreamer's.20 His interior currents seem to feed into his flood of words, as if his “complaynte” (487) were merely another form of fluid in his body's fungible economy of humors.21 The precise description of anatomy recalls Chaucer's account of the death of Arcite in the Knight's Tale, positioning the Black Knight almost at the point of death. Chaucer's assertion that the Black Knight's face is “Ful pitous pale and nothyng red” (470) anticipates an earlier description of the dead body of Seys “That lyeth ful pale and nothyng rody” (143), increasing the urgency of his predicament. The Dreamer's physical infirmity pales—so to speak—in comparison to the Black Knight's sickness.It soon becomes clear that in spiritual terms, too, the Black Knight is in peril. As we recall Chaucer's characterization of the Dreamer's malady as non-creative humanist melancholia, we may begin to read the Black Knight's illness as another form of melancholia—one spiritual rather than intellectual in nature. While the Dreamer's melancholia is Petrarchan, the Black Knight's malady is more elusive. To be sure, it is easily characterized as lovesickness, yet other clues provide a more nuanced reading. Though the “compleynt” the Black Knight utters just before he meets the Dreamer is short and uninspired, its existence suggests that he does not suffer from stunted creativity in the way the Dreamer does. Instead, the Black Knight's grief has reached the point of despair: he fails to imagine solace from anyone or anything. Without hope, the Black Knight laments, “No man may my sorwe glade,That maketh my hewe to falle and fade,And hath myn understondynge lornThat me ys wo that I was born!May noght make my sorwes slyde,Nought al the remedyes of Ovide,Ne Orpheus, god of melodye,Ne Dedalus with his playes slye;Ne hele me may no phisicien,Noght Ypocras ne Galyen;Me ys wo that I lyve houres twelve.”(563–73) Reflecting the Dreamer's negating lament at the poem's start, the Black Knight's list of failed sources for consolation includes ancient authors, mythical figures, and physicians. Nowhere does he imagine spiritual comfort from God or pastoral care from a priest through the sacrament of confession. In this, the Black Knight is guilty of acedia. The Dreamer's cryptic remark to the Black Knight later in the poem, “Me thynketh ye have such a chaunce/As shryfte wythoute repentaunce” (1113–14), reflects the latter's failure to understand the gravity of his spiritual His to imagine comfort from God suggests a of and the Black Knight is in condition than the Dreamer. title: Nature and Sociology ‐ by Newton, T.
abstract: Newton T . Nature and Sociology . Abingdon : Routledge 2007 vi + 212pp . £23.99 IBSN 978 0 415 36683 (pbk) From its inception, sociology has traded with a product specification which distances it from biology. In Nature and Sociology, Tim Newton argues that this overdraws the distinction; the biological is simultaneously social. As a result, he argues ‘to ignore our biology is to circumscribe our understanding’. Although we can separate sex from gender, race from ethnicity or disease from illness, ‘intercorporeality’ (you must excuse Newton here) lies at the root of much social interaction and thus human culture. Moreover, the new genetics is arguably undermining biology as ‘foundational’, with the production of knowledge that suggests ‘rewritable scripts’– flexibility rather than fixed structures. Nature and sociology meet at various intersections in this arena. Having said this, Newton spends most of the first part of Nature and Sociology examining the limits of social constructionism. The ‘brute facts’ of nature frequently resist such depiction. As Searle has pointed out, a realist view rests on the perception that the natural world existed before humans appeared on the earth, and has a reality separate from our (changing) characterisations and constructions. Our understandings require difference reference structures. Sociology cannot explain the dynamics of sub atomic particles, or how cells divide, though it might have interesting things to say about the disciplines that can. Similarly, and to paraphrase Geertz, genetics is silent on the housing market, or on doctors’ pay. Rightly, I think, Newton examines critically the limits of ‘anti-dualism’ where superficial attempts are made to integrate all forms of knowledge (about disease and illness, or the body, emotions and society) into a more ‘holistic’ project. Drawing on Hacking's work, Newton notes the difference between ‘indifferent and interactive kinds’ most succinctly summarised, surely, by Geertz’ famous observation that a blink is not a wink. Newton also criticises the superficial reading of the historical record in which Descartes, Christianity and even the ‘enlightenment project’ (strange, this one, given the critical metaphysics of Kant alone) are condemned tout court by sociologists arguing for a more integrated model. Newton states: ‘the desire to break down the barriers . . . manoeuvres our attention away from entertaining thoughts of difference between the social and natural terrain’. The second part of the book focuses on time, language and technology. Following Elias, Newton explores similarities and irreducible differences between time in nature and time in the social world. In nature, change typically takes thousands (if not millions) of years; in society wholesale restructuring can occur rapidly. Think, for example, of the transformations in social structure in Europe (East and West) in the last 30 years. By contrast, DNA, carbon or the boiling point of water remain stable over millennia. Nevertheless, Newton wants to hold on to the view that scientific knowledge of nature is ‘contingent and partial’ in its grasp of such phenomena, if only because our understanding of such processes are historically specific. Similarly, in the field of language and technology, whilst it is true that humans have achieved (or been cursed with) ‘symbolic emancipation’ (Elias once again) which separates them from the determinism of ‘unrehearsed or innate signals’ we remain ‘interwoven’ with the natural world. Medical sociologists might think here of Roy Porter's vivid description of the agricultural revolution, where many of the worst human diseases developed as the result of growing proximity to animals. And, whether we like it or not, technological developments under conditions of modernity bring us face to face with the limits as well as the malleability of the natural world (atomic waste, global warming, iPod batteries that won't decay). Newton pursues the debates that have ensued about the distinction between the natural and social worlds (and thus the natural and social sciences) by looking at theorists such as Margaret Archer and Nancy Cartwright. What results is a picture in which even long term and stable social processes, such as demographic change, can be combined with rapid events. For example, whilst it is unlikely that fertility in developed (and increasingly developing) countries will increase significantly in any foreseeable future, rapid decline among those countries with high rates has certainly occurred. Indeed the relative stability and secular character of ageing societies are themselves a product of fast changing social behaviour; notably contraception and economic participation among women in their reproductive years. Here, aspects of ‘corporeality’ are open to technical and symbolic forces which act as drivers of change, despite the stability of the natural processes that result in humans being born over and again by the million. Similar issues are explored with respect to genomics and neuroscience in the last part of the book. The limits as well as possibilities in refashioning bodies, needs and desires through biotechnologies are weighed in the balance. There are also cautionary comments about reductionism present in some recent sociological writings on gender and on the body, stress and health. What emerges from Newton's discussion is a fascinating picture of the interplay of the natural and social worlds, and the need to recognise at key points their differences. As the late, great biologist, Ernst Mayr has argued, each level (gene, organism, individual, group) has its own form of organisation, and needs its own form of study. ‘Linear links’ between the levels cannot easily be demonstrated. Whilst Newton does at times (he admits) want to have his ‘holistic’ cake and eat it with constructionists and realists alike, an ‘integrated’ view is finally resisted. And, while ‘ifs’ and ‘buts’ occur with a frequency that sometimes irritates, the overall result is an assured, insightful and intelligent book.

title: An Interview with Emily Rubin
abstract: You have accessThe ASHA LeaderFeature1 Jan 2011An Interview with Emily Rubin Carol MurphyMA, CCC-SLP Carol Murphy Google Scholar More articles by this author , MA, CCC-SLP https://doi.org/10.1044/leader.FTR5.16012011.np SectionsAbout ToolsAdd to favorites ShareFacebookTwitterLinked In http://www.asha.org/Publications/leader/2011/110118/An-Interview-with-Emily-Rubin.htm The alarming rise in the incidence of children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) is well known. The Autism Society of America posted the following statistics on its website about the impact in the United States: ASD prevalence is estimated at 1 in 110 births 1 to 1.5 million Americans live with ASDs ASD is the fastest-growing developmental disability There is 10%–17 % annual growth in the number of children diagnosed with ASDs $60 billion is the estimated annual cost in health care services and productivity, 60% of which are in adult services In 10 years, the annual cost will be $200–400 billion (Autism Society of America, 2010) The most important statistic for speech-language pathology is that the cost of lifelong care can be reduced by two-thirds with early diagnosis and intervention (Prizant, Wetherby, Rubin, Laurent, & Rydell, 2006). I have read about the various treatment methods for children with ASDs and have been fascinated with the range of approaches. One of the leading learning system curriculums, developed over a long period of time, is the SCERTS Model®. The acronym refers to the focus on: SC: Social communication—the development of spontaneous, functional communication, emotional expression, and secure and trusting relationships with children and adults. ER: Emotional regulation—the ability to maintain a well-regulated emotional state to cope with everyday stress, and to be most available for learning and interacting. TS: Transactional support—the development and implementation of supports to help partners respond to the child–s needs and interests, modify and adapt the environment, and provide tools to enhance learning (e.g., picture communication, written schedules, and sensory supports). Specific plans are also developed to provide educational and emotional support to families and to foster teamwork among professionals (Prizant, Wetherby, Rubin, Laurent, & Rydell, 2006). The SCERTS Model includes a well-coordinated assessment process that helps a team measure the child–s progress and determine the necessary supports to be used by the child–s social partners (educators, peers, and family members). This assessment process ensures that: Functional, meaningful, and developmentally appropriate goals and objectives are selected. Individual differences in a child–s style of learning, interests, and motivations are respected. The culture and lifestyle of the family are understood and respected. The child is engaged in meaningful and functional activities throughout the day. Supports are developed and used consistently across partners, activities, and environments. A child–s progress is systematically charted over time. Program quality is measured frequently to assure accountability. I met one of the SCERTS creators, Emily Rubin, whose private practice in Carmel, Calif., is dedicated to helping children with ASDs. We met an individualized education program (IEP) meeting; both of us were involved the treatment of the student. Rubin–s vast knowledge and speaking ability reflected her deep concern and understanding of the student and of all those affected by autism. After that meeting, I wanted to learn more and requested an interview. Q: Can you explain briefly what SCERTS is, where it came from, and how it evolved? The SCERTS model is a comprehensive, multidisciplinary educational approach designed for children with ASDs and their families. It was designed to provide guidelines for helping children progress through the stages of becoming a competent social communicator. It also was designed to provide families and educational teams with the help they may need to feel successful in supporting children. To ensure a child–s active engagement, there is a strong emphasis on preventing problem behaviors that interfere with learning and the development of relationships. Families and educational teams learn about essential interpersonal modifications, environmental arrangement, and visual supports and how they can be embedded in natural, functional, and meaningful contexts. The SCERTS Model collaborators include Barry M. Prizant, Amy M. Wetherby, and Amy Laurent. Collectively, the collaborators are trained in speech-language pathology, special education, behavioral and developmental psychology, occupational therapy, and family-centered practice. As collaborators, we embraced a range of evidence-based methodologies and perspectives, allowing families and service providers to draw from a wide range of effective practices in developing an IEP for a child. Q: How did your thinking about autism change in the course of the developing the SCERTS Model? When I first began working with children with autism, I remember focusing on each child–s stereotypical or repetitive patterns of behavior and considering these behaviors to be central to their disability. In doing so, I often neglected the function that they served for the child, simply discarding them as “autistic behaviors.” Since the development of the SCERTS Model, my perspective has changed. I now see many of these behaviors as an artifact of each child–s drive to cope with his or her feelings of uncertainty, anxiety, or even fear of social situations. As autism is a neurological disorder that makes it difficult for a child to predict the actions of other people, their ability to cope with social expectations in less predictable environments, make transitions, and use others a source of emotional support is often compromised. Thus, many children with autism are coping with a heightened degree of stress and have developed repetitive, soothing behaviors as coping behaviors. Although I used to ignore or discourage these behaviors, I have learned to understand their function, change my behavior in an effort to prevent these behaviors, and model replacement strategies that may be more socially appropriate and more effective. Similarly, when children with autism engage in more challenging behaviors, I have learned to move beyond the simplistic response of ignoring these undesirable behaviors to a more humbling process of recognizing that the antecedents may lie in my behavior, a variable that can easily be changed. For example, had I provided a clear and predictable end point, motivating and meaningful materials, and visual and organizational supports, the child may not have engaged in that challenging behavior. I also have learned that these moments of challenging behaviors present clear teachable opportunities for us to model emotional expression and appropriate coping strategies. Q: How do you see the SCERTS Model being used in the schools? Social communicative competence and one–s ability to engage in emotional regulation are predictive of positive long-term outcomes in all children, not just children with ASDs. Although the core academic curriculum that we target as educators is important, an individual–s ability to communicative effectively and demonstrate emotional maturity leads to that individual being more able to relate to others, establish peer relationships, and engage in positive social interactions. The SCERTS Model includes a social communication and emotional regulation curriculum within a formal assessment process that is criterion referenced from the 6-month to the 10-year developmental level. Thus, it can be used to select targets for any child who has difficulty in these areas and is under 10 years of age or is functioning developmentally within this range. Q: What aspects of SCERTS do you think fit into an integration of the social, emotional, behavioral, and academic parameters of other classroom goals? The social communication curriculum in the SCERTS Model is derived from longitudinal group research studies that have identified significant predictors of positive outcomes in language acquisition, oral expression, and verbal problem-solving. These developmental skills will likely bolster a student–s ability to access the academic curriculum in areas such as English language development, language arts, and reading. Similarly, the emotional regulation curriculum in the SCERTS Model is derived from longitudinal group research studies that have identified significant predictors of positive outcomes in self-regulation, organizational skills, and executive functioning. These aspects of a child–s development are similar to those addressed within the health curriculum content area and will likely bolster progress in all academic subject areas. Emily Rubin, MS, CCC-SLP is the director of Communication Crossroads in Carmel, Calif. She specializes specializing in autism, Asperger–s syndrome, and related social learning disabilities. She is an adjunct faculty member, lecturer, and member of the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Clinic at Yale University. Her publications focus on early identification of autism, contemporary intervention models, and programming guidelines for individuals with high-functioning autism and Asperger–s syndrome.
