title: 5th FIMSA International Congress of Immunology: Translational Immunology in Health and Disease
abstract: The 5th Congress of the Federation of Immunological Societies of Asia Oceania (FIMSA) was organized jointly with the 39th annual conference of the Indian Immunology Society (IIS) in New Delhi from March 14–17, 2012. Founded in 1992 as a non-profit scientific organization, the Federation currently has twelve immunology societies as its full members (Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Korea, Thailand, Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan, China, Sri Lanka, Iran, and India) and a few others as associate members. It is one of the four major Federations of the International Union of Immunological Societies (IUIS), the other three being the European Federation of Immunological Societies (EFIS), the Latin American Association of Immunology (ALAI: Asociación Latinoamericana de Inmunología), and the Federation of African Immunological Societies (FAIS). These Federations have played a key role in promoting collaboration and communication between immunologists through educational programs with the objective of advancing this science in Asia. The central theme of the FIMSA 2012 meeting was “Translational Immuno-logy in health and disease” with the focus of the main talks being applied research, broadly modeled on the bench-to-clinic theme. The Congress was followed by the FIMSA/IUIS/IIS Advanced Course on Basic and Translational Immunology (March 18–20, 2012) which was attended by 70 young scientists at the doctoral and post doctoral level. The Congress was attended by over 600 participants representing 31 countries with the bulk coming from the various states of India. A special effort was made to encourage the participation of young immunologists and post doctoral scientists by providing them bursary support and a platform for competitive presentation. The Congress was held in Hotel Le Meridien which provided an excellent scientific ambience. Situated in the heart of Delhi, very close to the historical monuments, and with the weather turning out to be brilliant, the week-long activity was a perfect blend of high science and social interaction. The Congress format was organized into 10 master lectures delivered by experienced researchers, nine theme-based symposia with 54 invited speakers and six parallel workshop sessions featuring 65 oral presentations selected from over 400 submitted abstracts. In addition, there were two dedicated poster review sessions. The program covered a wide range of important topics that included the immunological basis of autoimmune and infectious diseases including HIV and type 1 diabetes, cross talk between innate and adaptive immunity, immunodeficiencies, issues related to organ and bone marrow transplantation, immunological tolerance, tumor immunology, stem cells and regenerative medicine and new developments towards vaccine, immune diagnostics and cell therapy. The organizing committee introduced e-poster presentation at this Congress as an effective means of promoting peer networking and healthy discussion. Twelve computer stations were provided and these displayed the submitted posters in 3–4 screen pages each. The participants had the opportunity to view, at their convenience, the allotted posters of each day on big screens by clicking the poster number of interest; this also facilitated the discussion of the data with others and with the poster judges. Six best posters (2 for each day of the Congress) were awarded a cash prize and certificate during the valedictory ceremony. The awards were made available through a small grant from International Immunology (facilitated by the Editor-in-chief, Tadamitsu Kishimoto), which is published by Oxford University Press, on behalf of the Japanese Society for Immunology. An important highlight of the Congress was the session ‘Ten best oral presentations’, the participants of which were selected by a panel of international experts. Several awards were instituted to recognize the hard work put in by young researchers, with the ultimate goal being to promote excellence in research. Another important feature of the Congress was the ‘Round Table discussion’ session highlighting the issues related to ‘Gender equality and career development’. In addition to the scientific sessions, the meeting had a vibrant social program and an opportunity for the participants to experience traditional Indian hospitality and various facets of the diverse Indian culture. The registration fee of the Congress was kept affordably low, taking into consideration the difficult global economic situation and the cuts that have hit the research community in recent years. Fortunately, the meeting received crucial support from 7 government sponsor agencies and 18 private sponsors (http://www.fimsa2012.com). A pre-Congress press meeting was organized on the 14th March to which representatives of leading newspapers and electronic media were invited so that the general public could be briefed about the main features of the Congress. Narinder Mehra, the President of the Congress and his colleagues gave an overview of the meeting and the importance of immunology in health and disease. Stefan Kaufmann (President of IUIS) spoke about the importance of vaccines and immunotherapeutics in every day life and Nicholas King (FIMSA President) gave a perspective of the federation and of its various activities. The Congress was officially inaugurated by Sir Gustav Nossal (Australia), together with Stefan Kaufmann (President of IUIS, Germany), Nicholas King (FIMSA Presi-dent, Australia), GP Talwar (India), Jacob Natvig (Norway) and the organizers led by Congress President Narinder Mehra (Fig. 1 and 2). The inaugural and keynote address was delivered by Sir Gustav Nossal (Fig. 2A) who spoke on the development status of various vaccines and highlighted that immunology with its impact on human health could help prevent two-thirds of premature deaths, particularly those with an infectious cause. Interestingly while life expectancy at birth in the more developed world has improved from 70 years in the 1960s to >80 years in 2011, that in African countries (e.g. Zambia) has actually shown a decline from 45 to 39 years. Sir Gustav Nossal advocated the creation of a global fund for vaccine research for the three big diseases AIDS, TB and malaria. Further, he discussed the progress of the RV144 phase II trial of the prime boost vaccine ALVAL prime-AIDS; RTS,S from Glaxo Smith Kline for malaria; and three vaccines for TB currently in phase II trials namely, AERAS-402 crucell Ad35, MVA85 A/AERAS 485, GSKMT72, a recombinant fusion protein of Agtb 32 and tb 39. The first day of the conference started with a fantastic master lecture on peripheral regulatory T (Treg) cells by Abul Abbas (USA). He described how the immune system adapts to pathogenic inflammatory reactions by generating Foxp3+ve Treg cells in the periphery. A fraction of these cells survive as memory Treg cells and are able to limit subsequent inflammation in the tissue. He also showed that antigens and cytokines are the major stimuli that induce peripheral Treg cells and control their balance with effector cells. This was immediately followed by the second master lecture, which was given by James McCluskey (Australia) on the genetic control of immune response. James McCluskey talked about the extensive polymorphism in HLA molecules and the implication of this for determining immune response variables, and the risk of developing autoimmune disease, allergic reactions and HLA-linked drug induced hypersensitivity. The morning of the second day of the conference saw another wonderful series of master lectures, this time delivered by Rafi Ahmed (USA) and Stefan Kaufmann (Germany). Rafi Ahmed described the human B-cell response to influenza virus in people infected with the 2009 H1N1 pandemic strain and discussed the novel vaccination approaches for this virus which has been extensively discussed during the past decade. Stefan Kaufmann focused his lecture on host-pathogen interactions in tuberculosis. He described the novel vaccination strategies based on the improved rBCG strain which expresses listeriolysin but is devoid of urease. He showed that this candidate vaccine induces better protection and has proven to be safer than the wild type parental BCG. This vaccine has already successfully entered a phase II clinical trial. He highlighted the importance of biomarkers that could help to (i) discriminate latently infected individuals and patients with active TB, (ii) monitor clinical vaccine and drug trial, (iii) define mechanisms of disease pathogenesis, resistance and susceptibility and (iv) finally predict the risk of disease development. The close of the second day saw two more master lectures. One was given by Narinder Mehra (India) who highlighted the clinical relevance of antibodies in transplantation, the range of technologies for their detection and the importance of defining donor-specific and anti-HLA antibodies both in pre- as well as post-transplant stages. Narinder Mehra particularly stressed the potential role of antibodies to MICA, the molecule expressed primarily on endothelial cells, in transplantation. The other master lecture was given by Shigeo Koyasu (Japan) who presented studies on the type 2 innate immune response as predicted by natural helper (NH) cells. He described the role of these cells in lymphoid clusters in adipose tissues, termed fat associated lymphoid clusters (FACCs). The NH cells produce Th2 cytokines constitutively and support self renewal of B1 cells and IgA production by B cells. The concluding day of the Congress started with the master lectures by GP Talwar and Vijay Kuchroo. GP Talwar gave an overview of immunological approaches for the control of fertility through vaccination against human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which prevents unwanted pregnancy without impairment of ovulation and derangement of menstrual regularity. Recent studies by the Talwar group suggest that this vaccine is likely to have therapeutic applications in the treatment of hormone dependant cancers. Vijay Kuchroo (USA) highlighted T-cell subsets, particularly the IL-17-producing Th17 cells and their reciprocal relationship for the generation and induction of autoimmunity and FoxP3 Treg cells that inhibit autoimmune tissue injury. He discussed the specific nodal points in cellular differentiation that get activated during Th17-cell development. The last two master lectures of the Congress were delivered by Xuetao Cao (China) and Reinhold Schmidt (Germany). The former described the innate signaling pathways and their role in immune regulation. Xuetao Cao discussed TLRs and RLHs and the miRNA-mediated regulation of innate and adaptive immune response by IFN expression and signaling. Reinhold Schmidt described the role of autoantibodies in autoimmune diseases and defects in antibody receptor in immune response inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Reinhold Schmidt showed that the function of FcγR III and IV are each essential to trigger FcγR linker for activation of T-cell-dependent signals that drives C5a production in the Arthus reaction. The master lectures of the morning each day were followed by three parallel sessions of theme-based symposia. Symposium one focused on immune regulatory networks and started with the talk of Yousuke Takahama (Japan), who provided an overview of T lymphocyte repertoire formation in the selective thymic microenvironment. Following this, Hannes Stockinger (Austria) presented the work of his group on a new ultrasensitive live cell-imaging technique for studying immune reactions, which made effective use of the visualization of lipid rafts in living cells for the first time. Another speaker Paola Castagnoli (Singapore) highlighted the role of NFAT signaling in myeloid hematopoiesis and DC activation. An Indian scientist Subhadha Chiplunkar presented novel findings on Notch and its role in regulating the anti-tumor effector functions of γδ T lymphocytes. Joshy Jacob (USA) showed that CD28 expressed on T cells plays an important part in the regulation of short- and long-lived plasma cells. The last talk of this symposium was delivered by Satyajit Rath (India) who described the role of apoptosis-inducing factor (Aif) in regulating death in the T-cell lineage. The second parallel symposium focused on host-pathogen interactions and started with the talk of Guna Karupiah (Australia), who showed that tumor necrosis factor (TNF) plays an anti-inflammatory role in the host response to Ectromelia virus (ECTV) infection. The lecture of Gennaro de Libero (Switzerland) discussed thelarge number of T cells that recognize non-peptide antigens presented by non-MHC molecules, and the involvement of these T-cell populations in infections and their functional capacities. Thereafter three Indian scientists Dipendra K Mitra, Javed Agrewal and Natrajan Krishnamurthy working in the field of immunology of tuberculosis presented the results of their most recent work. Dipendra Mitra provided an overview of the T-cell response in human tuberculosis, Javed Agrewala showed that the lipidated promiscuous peptide restrains the progression of Mycobacterium tuberculosis by activating innate and prolonging adaptive immunity. Natrajan Krishnamurthy introduced the audience to the importance of calcium homeostasis during mycobacterial infection and presented a potential new strategy regarding adjunct therapy for drug resistant TB using S-amlodipine which may be a new player in the fight against multi drug resistant tuberculosis. Surasakdi Wongratanacheewin (Thailand) showed how a helminth parasite, Opisthorchis Viverrini, uses its antigens to modulate the host immune response by stimulating regulatory cytokines leading to evasion of the host immune response by and survival of the parasite. The theme of the third symposium was Treg cells, cytokines and inflammation, which started with a lecture by Bhagirath Singh (Canada) who highlighted the properties of two populations of Th17 cells — one being pathogenic and the other protective. In addition, Bhagirath Singh stressed the controversial nature of Th17 cells in autoimmunity. Cindy Mah (Australia) introduced a relatively recently identified T-cell subset, i.e. T follicular helper (Tfh) cells, a subset of CD4+ T cells that localize to B-cell follicles where they are positioned so as to provide help to B cells. Nicholas King reported that timed interference of specific leukocyte subset migration can significantly increase survival without compromising sterilizing immunity in lethal neurotropic flavivirus infaction. Sudhir Gupta (USA) and Vineeta Bal (India) discussed the impact of ageing on various cell lineages, including T lymphocytes and DCs. The fourth theme focused on tumor and transplant immunology. It started with a lecture by Jonathan Sprent (Australia) who discussed the expansion of T-cell subsets using IL-2-/mab complexes and the implications of such expanded T-cell subsets for immunity and transplant tolerance. Rajiv Khanna (Australia) presented that his group, in collaboration with an Australian biotech company (Cellestis Inc.), has successfully developed a novel T-cell-based immune monitoring technology (QuantiFERON-CMV) that allows the identification of high risk transplant patients i.e. those who may develop virus-associated complications post-transplantation. Catherine Fridman (France) showed that in human primary non small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs), the tumor microenvironment may impair NK cells locally, making them less prone to kill tumors and hence contributing to cancer progression. Nina Bhardwaj (USA) presented an overview of the tumor microenvironment and showed that tumors secrete factors that modulate both innate and adaptive immunity. Koji Nomota (Japan) introduced the role of probiotics as efficient immunopotentiators, describing their translational role in cancer prevention. Symal Roy (India) presented that the poor stability of peptide-MHC complexes may determine defective cellular immunity in Leishmaniasis. The topic of the fifth symposium was adjuvants and vaccines. During her talk, Olivera Finn (USA) supported the feasibility of vaccinating individuals at high risk for developing cancer in order to prevent its recurrence or progression. Nilabh Shastri (USA) described an antigen ‘Toxo’ derived from Toxoplasm gondi which is to be used as a new vaccine target for this eukaryotic parasite. Gregory Tsay (Taiwan) suggested that RNA interference targeting IL-10 is an effective strategy to silence the IL-10 pathway and has therapeutic potential that could be useful in the management of SLE and possibly other immune-mediated disorders. Chetan Chitnis (India) and Nirbhay Kumar (USA) presented their research work which is moving towards the development of a vaccine against malaria. Sunil Arora (India) highlighted one of the reasons for the success of antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis C infection which relates to the functional status of myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) in these patients. The sixth symposium covered the broad theme of autoimmunity, featuring discussions on the genetic and functional aspects of autoimmune diseases. Chella David (USA) and Kamal Moudgil (USA) unraveled novel aspects of autoimmune pathogenesis. The role of complement in RA and SLE, with a main focus on B-cell functions, was highlighted by Anna Erdei (Hungary). Veena Taneja (USA) described the importance of the interaction between the HLA gene products and gut microbes in the development of rheumatoid arthritis. Moncef Zouali (France) and Rahul Pal (India) gave an overview of new pathways and new targets in autoimmune diseases. The theme-based symposium of the last day of the Congress featured talks on immune mechanisms underlying infectious diseases. In this session, Miles Davenport (Australia) explained that the CD8+ T-cell response to viral infection involves the recruitment of multiple different T-cell clonotypes, each bearing a unique T-cell receptor. Nageshwar Rao (India) discussed the mechanism leading to immune suppression during the progression of leprosy from tuberculoid to lepromatous, namely the overproduction of CD4+CD25+/FoxP3+ cells. Padmini Salgame (USA) showed that the T helper and regulatory response induced by helminths could modulate the host protective response against M. tuberculosis. Suresh Mahalingam (Australia) highlighted the link between viral infections and inflammatory disease focusing on the Chikungunia virus. Symposium 8 started with a theme focused on infections, immunodeficiencies and HIV. The first speaker of this symposium, Rose Ffrench (Australia), presented data on the production of interferon-lambda in chronic HCV infection. This was followed by Gurvinder Kaur (India) who discussed the genetic architecture of HIV infection particularly in relation to disease susceptibility, progression and transmission. Gurvinder Kaur's lecture focused on three sets of immuno-regulatory molecules and their genetic polymorphisms, namely HLA, chemokines and cytokine gene polymorphisms. Stanley Schwartz (USA) linked the application of nanotechnology to HIV infection and Madhu Vajpayee (India) discussed the abnormal behavior of T cells in HIV. Ashok Kumar (USA) and Nirupama Trehanpati (India) focused on the immunology of ocular infectious disease and HBV infection in newborns respectively. The theme of the last symposium covered cell therapy using DCs, stem cells and NKT cells. Jose Villadangos (Australia) acquainted the audience with the cell biology of pathogen detection, processing and presentation by DCs. Similarly, Ram Raj Singh (USA) discussed the mechanisms and role of Langerhans cells in auto-immune skin inflammation. Dominique Charron (France) highlighted the challenges faced during stem cell therapy including allogenicity and immunogenicity. The last lecture of this symposium was delivered by Stephen Minger (UK) on the therapeutic and research potential of human stem cells. The afternoon session of the first day included three parallel workshops on immune regulatory mechanisms, infection, immunity, autoimmunity and tolerance. The workshop sessions of the third day were devoted to the topics of tumor and transplant immunology, vaccines, adjuvants and diagnostics. These sessions included short oral presentations selected from the submitted abstracts on a competitive basis and consisted mostly of young scientists presenting their research work. Uma Kanga as joint organizing secretary of the Congress put in a lot of hard work in getting more than 400 submitted abstracts evaluated according to specified criteria by about 40 senior immunologists drawn from various countries in the region. Based on the evaluations the abstracts were grouped into posters or oral presentations and, of the latter, those ranked in the top ten were included in a separate session. One of the highlights of the FIMSA 2012 Congress was the ‘Ten best oral presentations’ session in which 10 participants, selected by a panel of experts on the basis of their submitted abstracts, presented their work in the spirit of healthy competition. A panel of judges then selected the best three for an award of US$ 500 each, kindly made available by the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences (facilitated by the Editor-in-Chief, Douglas Braaten), which is published by Wiley on behalf of The New York Academy of Sciences. The awardees included Khalid Hussain Bhatt (India), Fatima Mami Chouaib (France) and Neeraj Kumar (India). The evening of the first day was occupied by a round table session on the very important topic of Gender Equality and Career Development and it was very keenly attended by a large gathering. The session was moderated by Olivera Finn (USA) and Narinder Mehra (India). Nirmal Ganguly (India) presented an overview of the global scenario with particular reference to the lack of opportunities to woman scientists, even in an advancing India. title: Evolutionary Medicine
abstract: Applying evolutionary concepts to medicine has ancient roots. Over two centuries ago, physician Erasmus Darwin recognized an understanding of adaptation and descent as helpful in medicine. This was before his famous grandson Charles Darwin saw diseases as evidence of heritable variation and penned his theory of evolution by natural selection. Over its history, however, evolutionary medicine has had some disturbing associations. Hijacked for unethical ideological ends including eugenics, forced sterilization, racism, and genocide by malevolent forces in Nazi Germany and elsewhere, Darwinian medicine's value and reception was undermined for many decades to follow. These nefarious chapters cast a long shadow, and for much of the twentieth century, evolutionary thinking had little influence within medicine, argue Peter Gluckman, Felicia Low, and colleagues in their 2011 perspectives paper in Evolutionary Applications. Now, though, as the world follows the emergence of ever-evolving COVID-19 viral variants, the cross-disciplinary field of evolutionary medicine is undergoing a renaissance. “Evolutionary medicine can help to reduce suffering and save lives. It is also full of new ideas, unexpected connections, and scientific surprises,” wrote Stephen Stearns in the inaugural issue of the journal Evolution, Medicine, and Public Health in August 2012. COVID-19 is one of many infectious diseases for which evolutionary thinking is helpful for individual and public health solutions. An evolutionary lens is also shedding light on antimicrobial resistance, cancer, cardiology, obstetrics, and psychopathology, to name just a few of its areas of influence. Medicine traditionally takes a reductionist, mechanistic approach to preventing or treating disease. Applying an evolutionary lens provides new ways of tackling difficult problems by focusing on ultimate—not just proximate mechanistic—causes. A scan of current research in evolutionary medicine hints at a much broader array of possibilities on the horizon. Barbara Natterson-Horowitz, codirector of the UCLA Evolutionary Medicine Program, uses evolutionary phylogenies to explore how cardiac disease and other human illnesses originated. Here, she examines a gorilla. Photograph: B. Natterson-Horowitz, MD. One area epitomizing an evolutionary problem is antimicrobial resistance. Antibiotics, explains Jacqueline Moltzau Anderson, propagate the modern medical idea of a quick fix: “You just take an antibiotic, and you're good to go,” she says. Overreliance on that quick fix “solution” has spurred global antibiotic resistance. Now, evolution is helping researchers find ways to tackle that problem beyond just developing new antibiotics, explains Moltzau Anderson, postdoctoral ­fellow in microbiology and immunology at the University of Michigan Medical School. Sid Thakur of North Carolina State University (standing) and Shivaramu Keelara, research assistant professor, NC State College of Veterinary Medicine, examine an XLT-4 plate to identify suspected salmonella bacteria. Photograph: John Joyner, NC State College of Veterinary Medicine. A color-enhanced scanning electron micrograph shows Salmonella typhimurium (red) invading cultured human cells. The extent to which these bacteria have evolved resistance varies geographically. Image: Rocky Mountain Laboratories, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health. “COVID will eventually go away, I hope, but drug resistance is not going anywhere,” cautions Sid Thakur, director of global health at the College of Veterinary Medicine at North Carolina State University. According to projections of the O'Neill Report, by 2050, 10 million people could die annually due to drug resistance, compared with 8.2 million of cancer. The reason, Thakur says, is simple. “We don't have antibiotics left on the shelves to deal with these pathogens, especially multidrug-resistant ones.” Most antimicrobial drugs were created 35 to 40 years ago. Now the pharmaceutical industry has little incentive to invest billions pursuing a new class of antimicrobials when pathogens become resistant the very next day. Because of hotspots where antibiotics are used without prescriptions, along with international mobility, surveillance programs must be global. Even informed by surveillance, however, with rapid microbial evolvability, it is inevitable that science is playing catch up. Thakur heads two surveillance programs. One is the genome sequencing based platform GenomeTrakr, launched by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2012. The second is the National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System, generating resistance profiles for bacterial pathogens in humans, food animals, retail meats, and seafood. Monitoring has shown that salmonella bacteria-resistance profiles vary geographically. For fluoroquinolones, an important class of antibiotics, salmonella collected from humans in the United States show a level of resistance of about 15%. In Southeast Asia, World Health Organization–funded research showed its resistance to be 85% to 90%. Selection pressures vary regionally, “and pathogens respond to that selection pressure,” Thakur says. Alexander Fleming, who discovered penicillin in 1928, warned that drug misuse could result in selection for resistant bacteria. But resistance long predates modern drugs. Resistant genes, explains Thakur, have existed for millennia, identified in different parts of the world. Although microbes may have simple genomes, their resistance mechanisms are complex. In teaching students about antibiotic resistance pathogens, Thakur compares what you would pack in a backpack for a hiking trip with what you would bring when going to class. When hiking, you carry a tent and other gear for traveling. When going to class, you do not need all that extra gear. “The analogy is that, when pathogens get exposed to antibiotics, which is harmful to them, they carry these extra genes, these extra plasmids.” The thought process has been that, when you take away the selection pressure—the antibiotics—“they will get rid of these genes and plasmids because they're very heavy; they cost a lot of energy.” But that is not what happens. Like ultramarathon runners, “they love to carry these heavy genes and plasmids, even in the absence of any antibiotics.” It improves their fitness, says Thakur. One strategy proposed in resistance hotspots has been to remove particular drugs from the population, assuming that evolution will go backward toward a more treatable form, making use of the original drugs more effective. “That actually has not been the case. Evolution has a difficult time going backward,” says Brandon Ogbunu, at Yale University. After completing medical school and a Fulbright scholarship to study malaria in Kenya, Ogbunu pivoted to conducting research in evolutionary biology. His work has revealed mechanisms such as compensatory mutations and has helped identify how and when we can expect evolution to be reversible. Evolutionary medicine looks beyond traditional rodent models to taxa such as chimpanzees and rhesus macaques to provide clues to human health and pathology. Understanding how immune system functioning differs between various nonhuman primates is important in making human comparisons. Photograph of chimpanzee: böhringer friedrich, CC BY-SA 2.5. Photograph of rhesus macaque: Horshadeep Saikia, CC BY-SA 4.0 International. Using experimental and field data, combined with computational and mathematical approaches, his research has revealed evolutionary consequences of small differences among people, drugs, and environment. “In the context of drug A or drug B, even subtle differences can have profound evolutionary consequences,” he says. Growing different mutant strains in the lab and using protein biochemistry and biophysics, he creates predictive models. His research suggests that a one-size-fits-all evolutionarily guided therapy is unlikely to be successful. Subtle differences between drugs, even similar ones, can have evolutionary consequences, offering perspectives for potential drug design. What we need to understand, says Ogbunu, is not just resistance but the evolvability of resistant variants, something front of mind during the COVID-19 pandemic. Ogbunu is also exploring the evolutionary rules that govern how a virus evolves strategies to infect as many hosts as possible. During her doctoral studies, Moltzau Anderson studied the human gut microbiome including its bacterial, fungal, and viral communities. To investigate what makes those communities resilient, she conducted experiments introducing a perturbation to understand whether the community would bounce back to a normal stable state. In a clinical setting, looking at inflammatory bowel disease, she also examined the impact on the microbiome of giving patients infected with Clostridium difficile a fecal transfer. Prior to her work, medical researchers suspected that the transferred bacteria restored health. However, after filtering out bacteria from the fecal material transferred, the treatment was still effective. What restores microbiome health after fecal transfer remains unclear, but one community hypothesized to be important are viruses. In the gut, “viruses are very beneficial,” she says. It's “perhaps an odd thing to say now with COVID going on… but the gut virome is very important in health and disease.” An evolutionarily informed examination of viruses also provides options in treating antibiotic resistant infections, explains Sandra Andersen, at the Center for Evolutionary Hologenomics, at the University of Copenhagen, Denmark. Whereas antibiotics are a bit like treating the body with a nuclear bomb, killing even the good gut bacteria and causing a lot of problems, “phage therapy is a super-targeted sniper,” she says. Phage therapy is an area making considerable progress. Phages, formerly called bacteriophages, are viruses that selectively target and kill bacteria. Phage therapy, over a century old, predates antibiotics but was abandoned for decades outside of Eastern Europe as the rest of the world's medical community fell in love with antibiotics. Biological anthropologist Jessica Brinkworth thinks about our immune system from an evolutionary standpoint, looking beyond traditional biomedical model systems such as mice and rats. Her comparative immunology in agricultural animals and nonhuman primates investigates how their immune systems compare with ours. Focused on severe infections and sepsis, a growing problem, she probes why not all individuals and species get sick. Examining four major clades of primates, humans, common chimpanzees, rhesus macaques, and olive baboons, Brinkworth's team examined susceptibility to infections by stimulating their blood with bacterial molecules and viral mimetics—a synthetic molecule that mimics RNA. Monitoring immediate immune response via whole-genome sequencing of blood leucocytes, she and colleagues found that humans and chimps mounted a “massive, scorched earth” response to bacterial and viral challenges, although the monkey response was much less powerful and more pathogen specific. For this specific immune challenge at least, “we are shockingly similar to chimps but less similar to Asian and African monkeys,” she says. That matters, explains Brinkworth, because our more distant relatives are often used as models in understanding human diseases. Another researcher looking beyond traditional model organisms for evolutionarily informed patterns in health and disease is Barbara Natterson-Horowitz, president of the International Society for Evolution, Medicine, and Public Health. Codirector of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Evolutionary Medicine Program and cross-appointed at Harvard University's Medical School and Department of Human Evolutionary Biology, Natterson-Horowitz studied evolutionary biology before medical training as a psychiatrist and cardiologist. While at UCLA, she began getting invitations from veterinarians to do cardiovascular consultations and diagnostics on zoo animals. It was an epiphany, she says, leading her to “tiptoe to the comparative side.” Her 2012 book Zoobiquity explored the intersection of human and veterinary medicine. She and collaborators use evolutionary phylogenies to explore patterns of origin in cardiac diseases including atrial fibrillation and atherosclerosis, as well as other human pathologies. In evolution, small things matter. Andersen studies the sociobiology of microbes including the ways in which they cooperate, compete, or cheat. She has explored how bacteria cooperate or cheat in the acquisition of iron, often a limited resource, by sending out iron-grabbing molecules. Microbes invest energy in producing these compounds, but some individuals cheat, stealing iron from their neighbors. Microbes not producing the iron-grabbing compound pyoverdine save energy, gaining a growth advantage. The action of these tiny pirates is visible in microscopic imaging because the iron-grabbing compound fluoresces bright green. Although her work is at an early experimental stage, it suggests an avenue for alternative therapy for bacterial infection: hijacking this iron-grabbing system by treating an infected individual with an alternative metal in a nontoxic solution. “Instead of binding to iron, it binds to this other metal that we put in. And it's very difficult for the bacteria to evolve resistance to this,” she says. By manipulating the social interaction of the bacteria, depleting its energy reserves, such compounds will not necessarily replace but could complement and aid antibiotics. Microbes have complex social lives, where they cooperate, cheat, and compete within and between species. When these dynamics play out inside our bodies, they may affect our health. Here, iron-grabbing molecules inside bacteria fluoresce bright green. Some bacteria produce their own iron-grabbing molecules, while some avoid this energetic cost by stealing from others. Photograph: Ashleigh Griffin. Understanding cheating at a microscopic level might give us an edge with cancer, too. If we think about our bodies as a cooperative multicellular system, “cancer is cheating in that system,” says Athena Aktipis, at Arizona State University. That frame changes the way we think about how cancer suppression mechanisms work, “how they take information and use that to decide what cells should or shouldn't do,” she says. It is an idea Aktipis explored in detail in her book, The Cheating Cell: How Evolution Helps Us Understand and Treat Cancer, and drives her lab's many projects examining cancer across species from sponges, mushrooms, and cacti to dogs and elephants. Part of a group called the Arizona Cancer Evolution Center, led by Carlo Maley, Aktipis cofounded the International Society for Evolution, Ecology, and Cancer, premised on the idea that many fields of study bring something to the table. title: Does the New World Order Worship Satan?
abstract: The economics and sociology literature that deals with churches and sects can provide a valuable framework when considering certain conspiracy theories. This article looks at two aspects of the so-called “QAnon” conspiracy theory: first, Q's theory on the elites; and second, Q's followers—the Anons—and their social structure. For the first, I examine the historical precedent for Q's theory and show how Iannaccone's “sacrifice and stigma” model can help frame the ideas in the theory.1 Concerning the second, I look to Iannaccone's church–sect model to explain how rational individuals can join and be involved in conspiratorial social network groups at both the church and sectarian levels.2Sunstein and Vermeule define conspiracy theories as “an effort to explain some event or practice by reference to the machinations of powerful people, who attempt to conceal their role (at least until their aims are accomplished).”3 While some conspiracy theories may prove true, others are false and potentially harmful, and still others are false and harmless. “Conspiracy theories often attribute extraordinary powers to certain agents [these powerful people]—to plan, to control others, to maintain secrets, and so forth”—and maintaining secrets in open societies can be very difficult, especially for government officials.4 However, if a conspiracy can be seen as requiring membership in an elite club to accomplish the goals of the conspiracy, then the question arises, can a conspiracy become sustainable?Q (also known as “Q Clearance Patriot”) first posted on 4chan on October 28, 2017; his “final” post (4953) was on December 8, 2020, a few weeks after the U.S. presidential election. However, a few more Q posts were posted during June 2022.5 Q hinted that he was in the military with high-level security clearance and working in close coordination with President Trump. Q post 1966 suggests that Q is not an individual but a team. Some have suggested that Q's postings are a psychological operation to keep the right in line, a live action role play (LARP), a deep state operation, and so on.6Q posits that a cabal of elites worldwide is controlled by three “puppet masters”7 and that this elite cabal advocates for a “New World Order,” worships Satan (Q post 133), and uses satanic symbolism (Q post 189). Q further suggests that children are sex-trafficked for these elites (Q posts 748 and 1880), that many have child sex slaves (Q posts 1213 and 1214), and that children abducted from third-world countries are used in satanic rituals including child sacrifice (Q posts 29 and 4914). Moreover, Q provides a long list of elites from both major U.S. political parties, Democratic and Republican, who are allegedly involved in molesting children, soliciting sex from minors, pedophilia, and so on, and who consequently succumb to blackmail by the Cabal, a secret group of powerful persons united by specific goals, which forces compliance with the Cabal's standards (Q posts 4630–4633). Many times, Q has predicted that if the things the Cabal has engaged in were made known, “none of them will be able to walk down the street” (Q posts 953, 3815, and 1328). Further, the arrests of child sex traffickers Jeffry Epstein8 and Ghislaine Maxwell and their links to the political class around the world have for many added credibility to Q's theory and increased the popularity of “QAnon.”9In this article, I extend the rational choice framework, something that has not been done so far, to what has been termed the “Q-Anon baseless conspiracy theory.”10 I do this in two parts: First, I examine whether Q's portrayal of the elites and their conspiracy (as just described) fits within the sacrifice and stigma framework.11 Second, I assess whether the church–sect framework can account for the behavior of the Anons and other followers of Q.12 “QAnon” was coined to lump together Q and his posts with the anonymous followers of Q in various social media spaces.The article proceeds as follows: The second section contains a literature review of QAnon. The third section uses club theory to model Q's narrative on the elites. The fourth section looks at the cost of joining elite clubs via human and child sacrifice in human history. The fifth section looks at the benefits provided by joining the Cabal. The sixth section applies the church–sect model to the Anons, with the seventh section applying the four propositions. The eighth section concludes the article.The literature on QAnon is diverse, with articles written in various journals and on various subjects. Peer-reviewed QAnon articles have appeared in sociology journals, psychology journals, social media and communication journals, political science journals, anthropology journals, terrorism journals, and religion journals. Perusing the titles and abstracts of the articles indicates they are overwhelmingly negative about QAnon. Further, many of the articles were not data-oriented in their analysis, though a few of them did try to collect survey data, analyze social media posts, and so on. In the literature, QAnon has been linked to various issues, including President Trump, COVID-19, election fraud, the Capital riot, other conspiracies, violence, religious cults, and so on.13 None of the papers seem to have approached the topic of QAnon from a rational choice perspective using the economics and sociology of religion literature. This article fills the gap. In this section, I review the more data-oriented literature. Additionally, the rest of the article cites the literature as appropriate.A ProQuest search on December 2, 2021, found numerous academic publications discussing “QAnon”: 184 scholarly articles and 24 dissertations and theses. When rerunning the search on September 6, 2023, the numbers had further increased to 526 scholarly articles and 88 dissertations and theses.Figure 1 shows us the popularity of QAnon outside the academic space. Further, the figure shows the number of narratives surrounding QAnon starting from the time Q first posted on 4chan,14 a webpage where people post images and comments on various topics. I used Google Trends to track keyword searches and produce a trend line. The line shows search interest in “QAnon” over time. We can see that interest in “QAnon” increased dramatically in 2020 and 2021, whereas interest was relatively flat with a few minor peaks during the first two years of postings. The Google Trends data points are normalized between 0 and 100, with 100 being the maximum search interest for the time and location selected. Results were filtered for the Web search category. Google Trends also shows spikes in the data that indicate a sudden increase of search interest in a topic. The Google Trends data is plotted in the secondary y-axis, with the x-axis showing the date.ProQuest is a database that tracks the number of documents—articles, trade journals, scholarly journals,
